23456.m: Birch tar was a kind of Stone Age glue.

23457.q: What is the period Ötzi lived in called?
23457.e: In Ötzi's time the first copper tools appeared. That is why it is called the Copper Age.
23457.m: Ötzi lived in the Copper Age.

23458.q: From which present-day country did the copper for Ötzi's axe come?
23458.e: Tests show that the copper came from Tuscany. Tuscany is in Italy.
23458.m: The copper for Ötzi's axe came from Tuscany.

23459.q: What colour does copper turn when it is left outside for a long time?
23459.e: Over time, copper gets a green layer. It is called patina.

23460.q: What is special about Ötzi's copper axe?
23460.e: From this time, otherwise only blades without handles have been found. On Ötzi's axe, the wooden handle has survived completely.
23460.m: Ötzi's axe has survived with its wooden handle.

23461.q: What do you call a mixture of two metals, such as bronze?
23461.e: When metals are melted together, you get an alloy. Bronze is one of the oldest alloys.
23461.m: A mixture of metals is called an alloy.

23462.q: Which metal do you need the most of to make bronze?
23462.e: Bronze is made of about nine parts copper and one part tin.
23462.m: Bronze contains a lot of copper and a little tin.

23463.q: What is bronze like compared with pure copper?
23463.e: The tin makes the metal harder. That is why bronze tools were better than copper ones.

23464.q: What is the period named after the metal bronze called?
23464.e: In the Bronze Age, people made many things out of bronze. In Switzerland it began around 4,200 years ago.
23464.m: The Bronze Age is named after the metal bronze.

23465.q: Which period came after the Bronze Age?
23465.e: Later, people learnt how to make iron. That is why the Iron Age came next.
23465.m: After the Bronze Age came the Iron Age.

23466.q: Which place in a sports competition gets a bronze medal?
23466.e: Gold is for first place and silver for second. Bronze is for third place.
23466.m: The bronze medal is for third place.

23467.e: Bronze shines golden brown. It is a little lighter than pure copper.

23468.q: Why was tin so valuable in the Bronze Age?
23468.e: Tin was only found in a few places. That is why traders brought it from far away.
23468.m: Tin was rare and had to come from far away.

23469.q: What was made from bronze in the Bronze Age?
23469.e: Weapons, tools and jewellery were made of bronze. For example swords, axes and arm rings.
23469.m: In the Bronze Age, tools, weapons and jewellery were made of bronze.

23470.q: What is the craftsman who works metal called?
23470.e: A blacksmith makes tools, weapons and jewellery out of metal. He works with fire and a hammer.

23471.q: On which heavy block does the blacksmith place the hot metal?
23471.e: The anvil is a heavy block of metal. On it, the blacksmith hammers the metal into shape.
23471.m: The blacksmith hammers on the anvil.

23472.q: What does the blacksmith use to hold the glowing metal?
23472.e: The metal is far too hot to touch. So the blacksmith uses long tongs.
23472.m: The blacksmith holds hot metal with tongs.

a: To blow air into the fire
23473.e: Bellows push air into the fire. That makes the fire much hotter.

23474.q: What was burnt in the smelting furnace to make it very hot?
23474.e: Charcoal burns much hotter than ordinary wood. With it, metal could be melted.
23474.m: Charcoal makes a very hot fire.

23475.e: The liquid bronze went into a mould made of stone or clay. As it cooled, it became hard and took on the shape.
23475.m: Liquid metal is poured into a mould.

23476.q: What was metal melted in, inside the furnace?
23476.e: A crucible is a small clay container. It can stand great heat.
23476.m: Metal is melted in a crucible.

23477.q: At about what temperature does copper become liquid?
23477.e: Copper only melts at about 1,085 degrees. An ordinary campfire is not hot enough for that.
23477.m: Copper only melts at over 1,000 degrees.

23478.q: What does a blacksmith do with a hammer?
23478.e: Glowing metal is soft. With the hammer, the blacksmith beats it into the right shape.
23478.m: The blacksmith shapes hot metal with a hammer.

23479.q: How did people pay before there were coins?
23479.e: In the past, people swapped grain for a tool, for example. This is called barter.

23480.q: Where were the first coins made?
a: In Lydia in what is now Turkey
23480.e: The first coins were made in the kingdom of Lydia. This country lay in what is now Turkey.
23480.m: The first coins came from Lydia.

23481.q: About how many years ago were the first coins made?
23481.e: The first coins were made around 600 BC. That is about 2,600 years ago.
23481.m: Coins have existed for about 2,600 years.

23482.q: What material were the first coins made of?
23482.e: The first coins were made of a mixture of gold and silver. Metal is valuable and lasts a long time.

23483.q: How did the picture get onto a coin?
23483.e: The metal was placed between two dies. Then it was struck with a hammer and the picture was pressed in.
23483.m: The picture is stamped into a coin.

23484.q: Which coins did the Celts copy for their gold coins?
23484.e: The Celts knew the gold coins of a Greek king from Macedonia. They made their own coins based on them.
23484.m: Celtic gold coins were modelled on Greek ones.

23485.q: How did the Celts make their potin coins?
23485.e: Potin is a mixture of copper, tin and lead. The Celts cast coins from it in moulds.

23486.q: Why was a coin more practical than swapping?
a: It was small and easy to carry
It was always made of pure gold
It was bigger than the goods
23486.e: You cannot put a cow in your pocket. Coins are easy to take with you and to count.
23486.m: Coins are small and easy to carry.

23487.q: In which Swiss city was a big lump of Celtic coins melted together found?
23487.e: The Zurich potin lump is made of many Celtic coins stuck together. It was found in Zurich in 1890.
23487.m: A lump of Celtic coins was found in Zurich.

23488.q: What was the Celtic tribe that lived in the area of Switzerland called?
23488.e: The Helvetii were Celts. They lived in the Central Plateau of what is now Switzerland.
23488.m: The Helvetii were Celts in Switzerland.

23489.q: What does the “CH” on Swiss cars stand for?
23489.e: Confoederatio Helvetica is the Latin name for Switzerland. The name recalls a Celtic tribe that lived here.

23490.q: What did the Celts build the walls of their houses from?
23490.e: The walls were made of wooden poles and woven branches. Clay was spread over them to make them tight.
23490.m: Celtic houses had walls of wood and clay.

23491.q: Which drink did rich Celts like to buy from the south?
23491.e: Rich Celts bought wine from Italy and Greece. It came in large clay jars called amphorae.
23491.m: Rich Celts liked to drink wine from the south.

23492.q: What was in the middle of a Celtic house?
23492.e: The fire in the middle gave warmth and light. Food was cooked on it too.
23492.m: The fire burnt in the middle of the house.

23493.q: What do you call a large Celtic town protected by walls?
23493.e: An oppidum was a large settlement with a rampart and wall. In Switzerland, for example, there was one on the Engehalbinsel in Bern.
23493.m: An oppidum is a protected Celtic town.

23494.q: How did most Celts make a living?
23494.e: Most Celts were farmers. They grew grain and kept cows, pigs and sheep.

23495.q: How did the Celts protect their villages?
23495.e: Many villages had a fence of wooden stakes or an earth rampart around them. That protected people and animals.
23495.m: Fences and ramparts protected Celtic villages.

23496.q: Who defeated the Helvetii in 58 BC?
23496.e: The Helvetii wanted to move to Gaul. The Roman Julius Caesar defeated them and sent them back.

23497.q: What was a druid among the Celts?
23497.e: Druids were priests and wise men. They knew a lot about the gods and the stars.
23497.m: Druids were priests and scholars of the Celts.

23498.q: Where did the druids often hold their ceremonies?
23498.e: The Celts had sacred groves. These are pieces of woodland where the druids held their ceremonies.
23498.m: Druids often held ceremonies in sacred woods.

23499.q: According to an old account, what did the druids use to cut mistletoe?
23499.e: The Roman Pliny wrote that druids cut mistletoe with a golden sickle.
23499.m: Druids cut mistletoe with a golden sickle.

23500.q: Which tree was especially important to the druids?
23500.e: The oak was a sacred tree. Mistletoe growing on an oak was thought to be very special.
23500.m: The oak was sacred to the druids.

23501.q: How did the druids pass on their knowledge?
a: They carved it on stone tablets
They wrote it in thick books
They painted it on cave walls
23501.e: The druids did not write their knowledge down. Their pupils had to learn everything by heart, often for many years.
23501.m: Druids learnt their knowledge by heart.

23502.q: According to a Roman account, what did druids not have to do?
23502.e: Julius Caesar wrote that druids did not have to go to war. They did not have to pay taxes either.
23502.m: Druids did not have to go to war.

23503.q: What did druids use their knowledge of plants for?
23503.e: Druids knew many plants and what they did. They used them to try to make sick people well.
23503.m: Druids healed the sick with plants.

23504.q: What is the druid in the Asterix comics called?
23504.e: In the comics, Getafix brews the magic potion for the Gauls. The character is based on a Celtic druid.
23504.m: Getafix is the druid in Asterix.

23505.q: According to Pliny, what colour were the druids' robes?
23505.e: Pliny described the druids wearing white robes when they cut mistletoe.

23507.e: The torc is open at the front. The two ends are often thick and beautifully decorated.
23507.m: A torc is open at the front.

23508.q: Who wore a torc among the Celts?
23508.e: A torc showed that someone was rich or powerful. Gods were also shown wearing torcs.
23508.m: A torc showed that someone was important.

23509.q: In which Swiss canton was a gold treasure with neck rings found in 1962?
23509.e: During building work above Erstfeld in the canton of Uri, seven gold rings were found. It is the Erstfeld gold treasure.
23509.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure comes from the canton of Uri.

23510.q: What are the rings of the Erstfeld treasure made of?
23510.e: The Erstfeld treasure from the canton of Uri is made of seven gold rings. The Celts hid it over 2,000 years ago.
23510.m: The Erstfeld treasure is made of gold.

23511.q: Where can you see the Erstfeld gold treasure today?
a: In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich
23511.e: The real rings are on display in the Swiss National Museum in Zurich. There are copies in Altdorf.
23511.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure is in the Swiss National Museum in Zurich.

23512.q: Who found the Erstfeld gold treasure?
23512.e: Two building workers were clearing away a rock with a digger. The rings slid out of the rubble.
23512.m: Building workers found the Erstfeld gold treasure.

23513.q: Among which people was the torc especially popular as a neck ornament?
23513.e: The torc is typical of the Celts. Even the Romans recognised Celts by their neck rings.
23513.m: The torc is a typical Celtic neck ring.

23514.q: What metal were most of the finds from La Tène made of?
23514.e: Most of the weapons and tools from La Tène are made of iron. The Celts were already good at working iron.
23514.m: Most finds from La Tène are made of iron.

23515.q: What was found in 1857 in shallow water at La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel?
23515.e: In 1857 a fisherman pulled many old iron weapons and tools out of the water there. They come from the Celts.
23515.m: Many Celtic iron finds were made at La Tène.

23516.q: Who made the first finds at La Tène?
23516.e: The fisherman Hans Kopp was searching on behalf of Colonel Friedrich Schwab. In a short time he found around 40 old weapons.
23516.m: A fisherman made the first finds at La Tène.

23517.q: Which weapons were found especially often at La Tène?
23517.e: Many swords and lance heads were found. Altogether around 2,500 objects came to light.
23517.m: Many swords and lances were found at La Tène.

23518.q: Why did even more finds come to light at La Tène later on?
a: The lake dried out in summer
A storm washed the sand away
23518.e: During the Jura water correction, the lake level was lowered by more than 2 metres. This left more of the site on dry land.
23518.m: The lower lake level brought new finds at La Tène.

23519.q: Which wooden structures were found at La Tène?
23519.e: The remains of two wooden bridges were found. They led over an old arm of the River Zihl.
23519.m: Celtic bridges stood at La Tène.

23520.q: What is the Celtic period named after the site of La Tène called?
23520.e: Researchers named a period of the Celts after this place. It began around 2,500 years ago.
23520.m: The La Tène period is named after a place in Switzerland.

23521.q: What is the museum that holds many finds from La Tène called?
23521.e: The Laténium is a large archaeology museum. It stands in Hauterive on the lake shore.
23521.m: Many finds from La Tène are in the Laténium.

23522.q: Roughly what does the name La Tène mean?
23522.e: The name means a place with shallow water. At the end of the lake, the water there was not very deep.

a: A grave under a mound of earth
23523.e: Earth and stones were piled up over the grave.
23523.m: A burial mound is a grave under a mound.

23524.q: What was often placed with the dead in a burial mound?
23524.e: The dead were given jewellery, weapons or pots. These things are called grave goods.
23524.m: Grave goods are things given to the dead.

23525.q: What does a burial mound look like from the outside?
23525.e: A burial mound looks like a small round hill. Today, trees often grow on it.
23525.m: A burial mound looks like a round hill.

23526.q: Where in Switzerland are many old burial mounds found today?
23526.e: In the forest, the mounds were not flattened by ploughs. That is why they are often still easy to see there.
23526.m: Many burial mounds lie in the forest today.

23527.q: Who studies old graves to learn more about the past?
23527.e: Archaeologists dig carefully and examine the finds. That is how we learn how people used to live.

23528.q: Who was given an especially large burial mound?
23528.e: A large grave with many grave goods showed that someone was rich and powerful. These are called princely graves.
23528.m: Large burial mounds belonged to important people.

23529.q: What does a Greek bronze vessel in a Celtic burial mound in the canton of Bern show?
a: That there was trade as far as the Mediterranean
That bronze was only made in Bern
23529.e: In 1851 a bronze jug from Greece was found at Grächwil. Goods like this came north along long trade routes.
23529.m: Finds from the south show old trade routes.

23530.q: Why are grave goods important for us today?
a: They show how people used to live
23530.e: Jewellery, tools and pots from graves tell us about everyday life. That is how we know a lot about people who had no writing.
23530.m: Grave goods tell us how people used to live.

23531.q: What was papyrus for writing made from?
23531.e: Papyrus is a plant that grows in marshes. The Egyptians made sheets for writing from it.
23531.m: Papyrus is made from a marsh plant.

23532.q: Where did the papyrus plant grow in Egypt?
a: On the banks of the Nile
In the middle of the desert
23532.e: Papyrus needs a lot of water. That is why it grew in the marshes along the Nile and in the Nile Delta.
23532.m: The papyrus plant grew along the Nile.

23533.q: Which English word comes from the word “papyrus”?
23533.e: The word “paper” comes from the Greek word “papyros”. That was the name of the plant from which the Egyptians made writing sheets.
23533.m: The word paper comes from papyrus.

23534.q: How were long papyrus sheets usually stored?
23534.e: People glued many sheets together into long strips. These were wound up into rolls.
23534.m: Long papyrus texts were stored as scrolls.

23535.q: How were the plant strips turned into a papyrus sheet?
23535.e: Thin strips of the plant were laid across each other in two layers. Then they were pressed and dried.
23535.m: To make papyrus, you lay strips crosswise and press them.

23536.q: Apart from writing sheets, what else did the Egyptians make from papyrus?
23536.e: Papyrus was very useful. People wove sandals, mats, baskets and ropes from it.
23536.m: The Egyptians also wove sandals from papyrus.

23537.q: Why have many old papyri survived until today?
23537.e: Egypt is very dry. So the papyrus often did not rot in tombs and in the sand.
23537.m: Egypt's dry air has preserved many papyri.

23538.q: Which part of the papyrus plant was used for writing sheets?
23538.e: The long stem was cut into thin strips. These were made into the sheets.
23538.m: Papyrus sheets are made from the stem of the plant.

23539.q: What did an Egyptian scribe always have with him for his work?
23539.e: The palette was a narrow board with hollows for the ink. The reed pens were kept in a slot.
23539.m: A scribe carried a writing palette.

23540.q: What did trainee scribes often practise on, because papyrus was expensive?
23540.e: Papyrus cost a lot. So for practice, people wrote on broken pieces of clay pots and on flat pieces of limestone.
23540.m: Trainee scribes often practised on pieces of pottery.

23541.q: Which two colours of ink did Egyptian scribes mostly use?
23541.e: Black ink was made from soot, red from red ochre. Red was used, for example, to highlight headings.
23541.m: Egyptian scribes mostly wrote with black and red ink.

23542.q: How did Egyptian scribes often sit while working?
a: On a chair at a desk
23542.e: Many statues show scribes sitting cross-legged on the ground. They held the papyrus on the stretched kilt over their knees.

23543.q: What is the oval called in which a pharaoh's name was written?
23543.e: The king's name was framed with an oval loop. That way it could be spotted at once in the text.
23543.m: A pharaoh's name is written in a cartouche.

23544.q: In which direction could Egyptian picture writing be read?
23544.e: People wrote from right to left, from left to right or from top to bottom. The animals and people in the script face the start of the line.
23544.m: Egyptian writing could be written in several directions.

23545.q: Who could read and write in ancient Egypt?
23545.e: Only a small number of people learned to write. That is why scribes were very important and respected.
23545.m: In ancient Egypt only a few people could write.

23546.q: What did scribes write down for the pharaoh, for example?
a: How much grain had been harvested
How many stars are in the sky
The names of the children playing in the village
Which fish swim in the Nile
23546.e: Scribes kept lists of harvests, taxes and supplies. That way the state knew how much grain there was.
23546.m: Scribes counted and recorded the harvest, for example.

23547.q: Which dangerous animals did cats keep away from Egyptian homes?
23547.e: Cats hunted not only mice but also poisonous snakes. That made them very useful in the house.
23547.m: Cats also protected the Egyptians from snakes.

23548.q: Why were cats so popular with farmers?
23548.e: Mice and rats ate the grain in the storehouses. Cats kept these animals away.
23548.m: Cats protected the grain from mice.

23549.q: What did the Egyptians often do with dead cats?
a: They threw them into the Nile
They left them lying in the desert
23549.e: Many thousands of cat mummies have been found. The cats were preserved and wrapped like people.
23549.m: In ancient Egypt many cats were mummified.

23550.q: According to the Greek writer Herodotus, what did families do when their cat died?
a: They ate nothing for three days
They moved to a new house
23550.e: Herodotus reported that the family shaved off their eyebrows in mourning. This shows how much cats were loved.
23550.m: Egyptians shaved off their eyebrows in mourning for their cat.

23551.q: What did the ancient Egyptian word for cat sound like?
23551.e: The word for cat was pronounced something like “miu”. It sounds like a cat's miaow.
23551.m: The Egyptian word for cat sounded like “miu”.

23552.q: What was the name of the ancient Egyptians' cat goddess?
23552.e: Bastet was often shown with a cat's head or as a cat. She protected home and family.
23552.m: Bastet was the Egyptians' cat goddess.

23553.q: Which wild cat are our pet cats descended from?
23553.e: The African wildcat lives in Africa and Arabia. It became tame and so turned into the house cat.
23553.m: Our pet cats are descended from the African wildcat.

23554.q: What kind of animal is a scarab?
23554.e: The scarab is a beetle. It is also called a dung beetle.

23555.q: What does the dung beetle roll along in front of it?
23555.e: The beetle shapes a ball from animal dung and rolls it away. It also lays its eggs inside it.
23555.m: The dung beetle rolls balls of dung.

23556.q: According to Egyptian belief, what did the beetle god Khepri roll across the sky?
23556.e: The Egyptians thought of the beetle with its ball. So they imagined that Khepri rolled the sun up into the sky every morning.
23556.m: The god Khepri rolled the sun across the sky.

23557.q: Why did many Egyptians wear small figures of a scarab?
23557.e: The scarab was seen as a sign of protection and good luck. So people wore it as an amulet.
23557.m: A scarab was a popular lucky charm.

23558.q: What else were scarabs with writing on the underside used for?
23558.e: Names or signs were carved on the flat underside. People pressed them into soft clay like a stamp.
23558.m: Scarabs were also used as stamps.

23559.q: Where was the heart scarab placed on a mummy?
23559.e: The heart scarab was placed on the chest near the heart. It was meant to protect the dead person in the afterlife.
23559.m: The heart scarab lay on the mummy's chest.

23560.q: What was the scarab a symbol of?
23560.e: Young beetles crawled out of the dung ball. That made the Egyptians think of new life and rebirth.
23560.m: The scarab stood for new life.

23561.q: What kind of body does the Sphinx of Giza have?
23561.e: The Sphinx lies there like a huge lion. Only the head is different.
23561.m: The Sphinx of Giza has the body of a lion.

23562.q: What kind of head does the Sphinx of Giza have?
23562.e: The Sphinx has the face of a human with a royal headcloth. People think it shows a pharaoh.
23562.m: The Sphinx has the head of a human.

23563.q: How was the Sphinx of Giza built?
23563.e: The workers chiselled the figure straight out of the limestone rock. Only a few parts were added with stone blocks.
23563.m: The Sphinx was carved out of the rock.

23564.q: What is missing from the face of the Sphinx of Giza today?
23564.e: The nose broke off many hundreds of years ago. It was about one metre wide.
23564.m: The Sphinx of Giza is missing its nose.

23565.q: Roughly how long is the Sphinx of Giza?
23565.e: The Sphinx is about 73 metres long and about 20 metres high. It is one of the largest statues in the world.
23565.m: The Sphinx of Giza is about 73 metres long.

23566.q: In which direction does the Sphinx of Giza face?
23566.e: The Sphinx looks east. That is where the sun rises every morning.
23566.m: The Sphinx faces the sunrise in the east.

23567.q: Which pharaoh probably had the Sphinx of Giza built?
23567.e: Most experts think the Sphinx was made in the time of Khafre. His pyramid stands very close by.
23567.m: The Sphinx probably dates from the time of Pharaoh Khafre.

23568.q: For a long time, what covered the Sphinx of Giza up to its shoulders?
23568.e: The desert wind kept blowing sand over it. Only in the 20th century was the Sphinx fully uncovered.
23568.m: For a long time the Sphinx was buried in sand up to its shoulders.

23569.e: Cleopatra ruled Egypt as pharaoh. She is one of the best-known women in history.

23570.q: Which number does the famous Cleopatra have in her name?
23570.e: There were other queens called Cleopatra before her. That is why she is called Cleopatra VII.
23570.m: The famous Cleopatra is called Cleopatra the Seventh.

23571.q: Which famous Roman was allied with Cleopatra and had a son with her?
23571.e: Cleopatra and Julius Caesar had a son called Caesarion. Caesar helped her stay queen.
23571.m: Cleopatra and Julius Caesar had a son together.

23572.q: With which Roman general did Cleopatra have three children?
23572.e: Cleopatra and Mark Antony had three children. Together they fought against Octavian.
23572.m: Cleopatra and Mark Antony had three children.

23573.q: In which city on the Mediterranean did Cleopatra have her palace?
23573.e: Alexandria was the capital of Egypt at that time. The city had a famous lighthouse and a great library.

23574.q: Which language did Cleopatra learn as the first ruler of her family?
23574.e: Cleopatra's ancestors had only spoken Greek. According to the historian Plutarch, she was the first in her family to also learn the language of the people of Egypt.
23574.m: Cleopatra was the first in her family to speak Egyptian.

23575.q: Where did Cleopatra's family originally come from?
23575.e: Cleopatra belonged to the Ptolemy family. They came from Macedonia in the north of Greece.

23576.q: Roughly how many years ago did Cleopatra live?
23576.e: Cleopatra lived from 69 to 30 BC. That is a little more than 2000 years ago.

23577.q: Roughly how long did Pharaoh Ramesses II reign?
23577.e: Ramesses II reigned from about 1279 to 1213 BC. That is about 66 years.
23577.m: Ramesses II reigned for about 66 years.

23578.q: Which nickname was Ramesses II given?
23578.e: Ramesses II built a lot and reigned for a very long time. That is why he is called Ramesses the Great.
23578.m: Ramesses II is also called Ramesses the Great.

23579.q: Against which people did Ramesses II fight at the Battle of Kadesh?
23579.e: The Hittites had a large empire in what is now Turkey. At Kadesh in Syria they fought against Egypt.
23579.m: Ramesses II fought the Hittites at Kadesh.

23580.q: What did Ramesses II later make with the Hittites?
23580.e: In 1259 BC the two empires made peace. The treaty is seen as the oldest known written peace treaty.
23580.m: Ramesses II made one of the oldest peace treaties in the world.

23581.q: Roughly how many sons and daughters of Ramesses II are known?
23581.e: About 45 sons and 40 daughters are known. Ramesses II had several wives.
23581.m: Ramesses II had over 80 known children.

a: In the Valley of the Kings
In the temple of Abu Simbel
In the Valley of the Queens
23582.e: Ramesses II was buried in a rock tomb in the Valley of the Kings. His mummy was later hidden and only found again in 1881.
23582.m: Ramesses II was buried in the Valley of the Kings.

23583.q: Who is shown by the four giant seated figures in front of the rock temple of Abu Simbel?
23583.e: Ramesses II had the temple carved into the rock. In front of the entrance sit four giant figures of himself.
23583.m: Ramesses II sits four times in front of the temple of Abu Simbel.

23584.q: How were the temples of Abu Simbel originally built?
23584.e: The workers chiselled the rooms and figures straight out of a sandstone mountain. That is why they are called rock temples.
23584.m: The temples of Abu Simbel were carved into a mountain.

23585.q: How many giant seated figures sit in front of the great temple of Abu Simbel?
23585.e: Four figures of the pharaoh sit in front of the entrance. Each one is about 20 metres high.
23585.m: Four giant figures sit in front of the great temple of Abu Simbel.

23586.q: Which pharaoh had the temples of Abu Simbel built?
23586.e: Pharaoh Ramesses II had the rock temples built. The four giant figures in front of the great temple show him.
23586.m: Ramesses II had Abu Simbel built.

23587.q: Why were the temples of Abu Simbel moved in the 1960s?
a: They would have sunk in a reservoir
They were in the way of a road
A king wanted them in Cairo
23587.e: The new Aswan Dam created a huge lake. The water would have flooded the temples.
23587.m: Abu Simbel was moved so that it would not sink in the reservoir.

23588.q: How were the temples of Abu Simbel moved to higher ground?
a: Lifted in one piece with cranes
23588.e: Workers cut the temples into over 1000 large blocks. Higher up, they put everything back together exactly.
23588.m: The temples of Abu Simbel were cut up and rebuilt.

23589.q: Where in Egypt is Abu Simbel?
23589.e: Abu Simbel is in the south of Egypt, close to the border with Sudan. The area is called Nubia.
23589.m: Abu Simbel is in the far south of Egypt.

23590.q: What happens twice a year in the great temple of Abu Simbel?
23590.e: In February and October the morning light falls through the entrance. It lights up the statues of the gods at the very back of the temple.
23590.m: Twice a year the sun shines deep into the temple of Abu Simbel.

23591.q: Which organisation helped rescue the temples of Abu Simbel?
23591.e: UNESCO called on many countries to help. Today the temples are World Heritage.
23591.m: UNESCO helped to save Abu Simbel.

23592.q: Every year the Egyptians measured how high the water in the Nile rose. What did this tell them?
a: Whether the harvest would be good
How many fish were in the river
23592.e: If the water rose enough, the fields got plenty of water and mud. Then there was a good harvest.
23592.m: The level of the Nile showed whether the harvest would be good.

23593.q: What did the farmers use to cut the ripe grain?
23593.e: A sickle is a curved knife. In the past, sickles often had sharp blades made of flint.
23593.m: The farmers harvested the grain with sickles.

23594.q: Where was the harvested grain stored?
23594.e: Granaries were buildings made of mud bricks. There the grain stayed dry and safe for bad years.
23594.m: The grain was stored in granaries.

23595.q: Which sweet fruits did the Egyptians harvest from palm trees?
23595.e: Date palms grew well along the Nile. The sweet dates were eaten fresh or dried.
23595.m: The Egyptians harvested dates from palm trees.

23596.q: How many seasons did the ancient Egyptian year have?
23596.e: There was the season of flooding, the season of sowing and the season of harvest. Each lasted about four months.
23596.m: The Egyptian year had three seasons.

23597.q: What is the device with a long lever that farmers used to lift water from the Nile called?
23597.e: A shaduf has a long beam with a bucket and a counterweight. This made it easy to lift water up.
23597.m: Farmers lifted water from the Nile with a shaduf.

23598.q: Which animals pulled the Egyptian farmers' plough?
23598.e: Cattle were strong and patient. They pulled the wooden plough across the fields.
23598.m: Along the Nile, cattle pulled the plough.

23599.q: The farmers had to give something to the pharaoh. What did they give?
23599.e: For a long time there were no coins. The farmers gave part of their grain to the state.
23599.m: Egyptian farmers handed over part of their harvest.

23600.e: Senet was played on a board with squares. It is one of the oldest known board games.
23600.m: Senet is an ancient Egyptian board game.

23601.q: How many squares does a Senet board have?
23601.e: The Senet board has three rows of ten squares each. That makes 30 squares altogether.

23602.q: In Senet, what decided how far you could move?
23602.e: Instead of a dice, people threw flat sticks or bones. The side that landed facing up showed the number.
23602.m: In Senet, people threw sticks instead of dice.

23603.q: How many people played Senet together?
23603.e: Two people played against each other. Each had their own pieces.
23603.m: Senet is played by two people against each other.

23604.q: Who played the board game Senet in ancient Egypt?
23604.e: Senet was popular all over Egypt. Ordinary people scratched the board into stone, while pharaohs had precious boards.
23604.m: Both poor and rich people played Senet.

23605.q: What did the Egyptians later think of when playing Senet?
23605.e: The game came to be linked with the journey of the dead to the afterlife. That is why Senet boards were often placed in tombs.
23605.m: Senet stood for the journey to the afterlife.

23606.q: Roughly how old is the game Senet?
23606.e: Senet pieces have been found in very early royal tombs. They are about 5000 years old.

23607.q: Which part of the face did the ancient Egyptians make up in a particularly striking way?
23607.e: In pictures and statues you can see thick dark lines around the eyes. This was typical of Egypt.
23607.m: The ancient Egyptians mainly made up their eyes.

23608.q: What is the black eye make-up called that the Egyptians already used?
23608.e: Kohl was made from a dark mineral. It was put on with a small stick.
23608.m: Kohl is a black eye make-up.

23609.q: What did the Egyptians make green eye make-up from?
23609.e: Malachite is a green rock. People ground it into powder and mixed it with fat.
23609.m: Green make-up was made from malachite.

23610.q: What else did dark eye make-up help with in ancient Egypt?
23610.e: The dark colour around the eyes reduced the glare in the strong sun. People also believed it protected against eye diseases.
23610.m: Eye make-up helped against the glaring sunlight.

23611.q: Who wore make-up in ancient Egypt?
23611.e: In ancient Egypt both women and men wore make-up. Pharaohs wore eye make-up too.
23611.m: In Egypt men wore make-up too.

23612.q: Who wore especially large and elaborate wigs in ancient Egypt?
23612.e: Large wigs made of real hair were expensive. So rich people used them to show how important they were.
23612.m: Large wigs were worn mainly by rich Egyptians.

23613.q: Why did many Egyptians shave their heads and wear wigs?
a: Because their hair did not grow
23613.e: Without their own hair it was cooler and cleaner. Then lice had nowhere to live.
23613.m: Wigs helped against lice and heat.

23614.q: What were good wigs made of in ancient Egypt?
23614.e: The best wigs were made of real human hair. Simpler ones were made of plant fibres.
23614.m: Good Egyptian wigs were made of human hair.

23615.q: What is in the Valley of the Kings?
23615.e: For about 500 years, pharaohs were buried in the Valley of the Kings. The tombs lie deep in the rock.
23615.m: The tombs of many pharaohs are in the Valley of the Kings.

23616.q: Near which modern city is the Valley of the Kings?
23616.e: The valley lies opposite Luxor. In the past the city was called Thebes.
23616.m: The Valley of the Kings is near Luxor.

23617.q: On which side of the Nile is the Valley of the Kings?
a: On the coast of the Red Sea
23617.e: The sun sets in the west. For the Egyptians, the west was the land of the dead.
23617.m: The Valley of the Kings lies west of the Nile.

23619.q: Which British explorer found a tomb full of treasures in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
23619.e: Howard Carter searched in the valley for many years. The search was paid for by Lord Carnarvon.
23619.m: Howard Carter found a famous tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922.

23620.q: Why were pharaohs buried in the Valley of the Kings instead of in pyramids?
a: To protect them from tomb robbers
Because the ground there was soft
23620.e: Pyramids stood out at once and were often robbed. The tombs in the rock were better hidden.
23620.m: In the Valley of the Kings the tombs were meant to be safe from robbers.

23621.q: Roughly how many tombs are known in the Valley of the Kings today?
23621.e: The tombs have numbers with the letters KV. More than 60 of them are known today.
23621.m: Over 60 tombs are known in the Valley of the Kings.

23622.q: What can you see on the walls of many tombs in the Valley of the Kings?
23622.e: The walls are painted with pictures of gods and with texts. They were meant to show the dead person the way to the afterlife.
23622.m: Many tombs in the Valley of the Kings are brightly painted.

23623.q: What did the early Egyptians build simple boats from?
23623.e: People tied many papyrus stems tightly together. Because the stems are light, the boat floated well.
23623.m: Early Egyptian boats were made of bundled papyrus.

23624.e: Feluccas are traditional wooden boats with a sail. They have sailed on the Nile for a very long time.
23624.m: A felucca is a wooden sailing boat.

23625.q: What shape is the sail of a felucca?
23625.e: Feluccas have a large triangular sail on a sloping pole. This lets them tack well against the wind.
23625.m: A felucca has a triangular sail.

23626.q: Where can you still see many feluccas today, for example in Aswan?
23626.e: In Aswan and Luxor, many feluccas sail on the Nile. Today travellers often go on trips in them.
23626.m: Many feluccas still sail on the Nile today.

23627.q: In which direction does the Nile flow?
23627.e: The Nile flows north from Africa into the Mediterranean. With the current, boats could easily travel north.

23628.q: Where does the wind in Egypt usually blow from?
23628.e: The wind usually comes from the Mediterranean. That is why boats could sail upstream well.
23628.m: In Egypt the wind usually blows from the north.

23629.q: Across which ocean did the explorer Thor Heyerdahl sail in a papyrus boat in 1970?
23629.e: His boat was called Ra II. He sailed it from Morocco to Barbados in the Caribbean.
23629.m: Thor Heyerdahl crossed the Atlantic in a papyrus boat in 1970.

23630.q: How did the Egyptians move boats forward when there was no wind?
23630.e: When there was no wind, men rowed the boat. Large ships had many rowers.

23631.q: Where did children in Mesopotamia learn to write cuneiform?
23631.e: The school was called the tablet house. There the pupils practised the signs for many years.
23631.m: Children learned cuneiform at a school for scribes.

23632.q: Roughly how many different signs did cuneiform have?
23632.e: Many signs stood for whole words or syllables. That is why several hundred different signs were needed.

23633.q: What could you do if you made a mistake on a damp clay tablet?
a: Throw the tablet in the fire
23633.e: As long as the clay was still damp, you could smooth it with your finger or a tool. Then you wrote again.
23633.m: Damp clay could be smoothed and written on again.

23634.e: Cuneiform began in the south of Mesopotamia. This people lived there in large cities.

23635.e: The first clay tablets with written signs are about 5300 years old. This makes cuneiform one of the oldest scripts in the world.
23635.m: Cuneiform is one of the oldest scripts in the world.

23636.q: What did people in Mesopotamia write cuneiform on?
23636.e: People pressed the signs into soft clay. Then the tablet was left to dry or was fired.
23636.m: Cuneiform was written on clay tablets.

23637.q: How big were most clay tablets with cuneiform?
a: About the size of a hand
As small as a grain of rice
23637.e: Most tablets fitted nicely in one hand. That way people could hold them while writing.
23637.m: Most clay tablets were about the size of a hand.

23638.q: What was used to press cuneiform into the clay?
23638.e: The stylus had an angular tip. It was used to press wedge-shaped signs into the soft clay.
23638.m: Cuneiform was pressed into clay with a reed stylus.

23639.q: What did people in Mesopotamia build their ziggurats from?
23639.e: There was little stone and wood in Mesopotamia, but plenty of clay. So people built with bricks made of mud.
23639.m: Ziggurats were built from mud bricks.

23640.q: What does a ziggurat look like?
a: Like a tower with large steps
23640.e: A ziggurat is a temple tower made of several levels. Each level is a little smaller than the one below.
23640.m: A ziggurat is a stepped tower.

23641.q: What stood at the very top of a ziggurat?
23641.e: A small temple stood on the top level. People believed that a god could live there or come to visit.
23641.m: A temple stood on top of the ziggurat.

23642.q: How did people get up a ziggurat?
23642.e: Long staircases led from the bottom to the top. The ziggurat of Ur had three staircases that met at the front.
23642.m: People climbed the ziggurat by wide staircases.

23643.q: To which god was the ziggurat of Ur dedicated?
23643.e: The ziggurat of Ur belonged to the temple of the moon god Nanna. He was the protecting god of the city.
23643.m: The ziggurat of Ur belonged to the moon god Nanna.

23644.q: Which story from the Bible may be a reminder of a ziggurat?
23644.e: Many researchers believe that a huge ziggurat was the model for the story of the Tower of Babel. Nobody knows for sure.
23644.m: The story of the Tower of Babel recalls a ziggurat.

23645.q: Which buildings from Egypt is the ziggurat often compared with?
23645.e: Both are big and have a similar shape. But the pyramids were tombs, while the ziggurat was a temple tower.
23645.m: The ziggurat looks like a pyramid but was not a tomb.

23646.q: What is left of most ziggurats today?
a: Only the temple at the top
23646.e: Mud bricks do not last for ever. Of most ziggurats, only the lower levels or remains are still standing.
23646.m: Only ruins are left of most ziggurats.

a: A king from an ancient legend
23647.e: Gilgamesh is the main character of a very old story from Mesopotamia. There was probably a real king with this name.
23647.m: Gilgamesh is a king from an ancient legend.

23648.e: Uruk was one of the largest cities of the Sumerians. In the legend, Gilgamesh builds a mighty city wall around Uruk.

23649.q: What is the name of Gilgamesh's best friend?
23649.e: Enkidu was at first a wild man who lived with the animals. Then he became Gilgamesh's loyal friend.

23650.q: What does Gilgamesh search for after his friend has died?
23650.e: His friend's death makes Gilgamesh very afraid. So he wants to find out how never to die.
23650.m: In the legend, Gilgamesh searches for eternal life.

23651.q: Which animal steals the plant of youth from Gilgamesh?
23651.e: Gilgamesh finds a plant that is supposed to make you young. While he is bathing, a snake eats the plant.
23651.m: A snake takes the plant of youth away from Gilgamesh.

23652.q: Which event does the wise Utnapishtim tell about in the Epic of Gilgamesh?
23652.e: Utnapishtim built a ship and so survived a huge flood. The story is very similar to the story of Noah in the Bible.
23652.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh contains a story about a great flood.

23653.q: Which creature of the goddess Ishtar do Gilgamesh and Enkidu defeat?
23653.e: The goddess sends the Bull of Heaven because Gilgamesh insulted her. The two friends kill the bull.
23653.m: Gilgamesh and Enkidu defeat the Bull of Heaven.

23654.q: Which guardian do Gilgamesh and Enkidu defeat in the Cedar Forest?
23654.e: Humbaba was a terrifying guardian of the Cedar Forest. The two friends defeat him and cut down the cedars.
23654.m: Gilgamesh and Enkidu defeat the guardian Humbaba.

23655.q: Which legendary queen are the Hanging Gardens sometimes named after?
23655.e: Greek stories linked the gardens with Queen Semiramis. She is mainly a figure of legend.
23655.m: The Hanging Gardens are also called the Gardens of Semiramis.

23656.q: How might the water for the Hanging Gardens have been brought up?
a: With a waterfall from the mountains
23656.e: Researchers think of bucket wheels or water screws that were turned by people or animals. The water came from the river.
23656.m: Water-lifting machines may have raised the water into the gardens.

23657.q: According to the old accounts, what did the Hanging Gardens look like?
23657.e: The plants grew on levels one above the other, like a green mountain. From below it looked as if the gardens were hanging.
23657.m: The Hanging Gardens were gardens on terraces one above the other.

23658.q: What do researchers still not know for sure about the Hanging Gardens?
23658.e: No reliable remains of the gardens have been found so far. That is why researchers argue about whether they really existed.
23658.m: Whether the Hanging Gardens really existed is still unclear.

23659.q: According to a legend, for whom did the king build the Hanging Gardens?
23659.e: According to the legend, the king wanted to give his wife great joy. So he had the gardens laid out.
23659.m: According to legend, the king built the gardens for his wife.

23660.q: According to legend, why did the queen want the Hanging Gardens?
a: She missed the green mountains of her homeland
She wanted to sell fruit there
She wanted to see the city from above
She wanted to hide from enemies
23660.e: The queen came from a land with mountains and forests. She did not like the flat, dry landscape.
23660.m: The gardens were meant to remind the queen of the mountains of her homeland.

23661.q: In that dry region, what did the Hanging Gardens need most of all?
23661.e: It rained very little there. The water had to be brought up from the river with great effort.
23661.m: The Hanging Gardens needed a lot of water.

23662.e: The Ishtar Gate was one of the entrances to a large city in Mesopotamia. A magnificent road led through the gate.
23662.m: The Ishtar Gate was a magnificent city gate.

23663.q: What colour are the bricks of the Ishtar Gate?
23663.e: The bricks shine a strong blue. On them you can see light and golden yellow animals.

23664.q: Which animals can be seen on the Ishtar Gate?
23664.e: On the gate you can see bulls and dragon-like mythical creatures. They stood for important gods.
23664.m: Bulls and dragons are shown on the Ishtar Gate.

23665.q: Which animals decorated the road leading to the Ishtar Gate?
23665.e: On the walls along the road there were many lions made of coloured bricks. The lion was the animal of the goddess Ishtar.
23665.m: Lions decorated the road to the Ishtar Gate.

23666.q: Which country did the researchers come from who excavated the Ishtar Gate from 1899?
23666.e: The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey led the excavation for many years. He found thousands of pieces of the coloured bricks.
23666.m: German researchers excavated the Ishtar Gate.

23667.q: Who is the Ishtar Gate named after?
23667.e: Ishtar was an important goddess in Mesopotamia. She was the goddess of love and war.
23667.m: The Ishtar Gate is named after the goddess Ishtar.

23668.q: What is the name of the magnificent road that led through the Ishtar Gate?
23668.e: At great festivals, processions in honour of the gods passed along this road and through the gate. That is how it got its name.
23668.m: The Processional Way led through the Ishtar Gate.

23669.q: What makes the bricks of the Ishtar Gate so shiny?
23669.e: The bricks were covered with a glass-like layer and fired. That is why they still shine today.
23669.m: A glaze makes the bricks of the Ishtar Gate shine.

23670.q: What is King Hammurabi famous for?
23670.e: Hammurabi had many laws written down. It is one of the oldest known collections of laws.
23670.m: Hammurabi is famous for his laws.

23671.q: What did Hammurabi have his laws written on?
23671.e: The laws are on a stone pillar over two metres high, called a stele. That way everyone could see them.
23671.m: Hammurabi's laws are on a stone pillar.

23672.q: What colour is the stone pillar with Hammurabi's laws?
23672.e: The pillar is made of a hard, dark rock. That is why it looks almost black.
23672.m: The pillar with Hammurabi's laws is black.

23673.q: In which museum is the pillar with Hammurabi's laws today?
23673.e: French researchers found the pillar around 1901. Since then it has stood in the Louvre in Paris.
23673.m: The pillar with Hammurabi's laws is in the Louvre.

23674.q: In which script are Hammurabi's laws written?
23674.e: In Mesopotamia people wrote with signs made of wedges. The laws were also carved into the stone like this.
23674.m: Hammurabi's laws are written in cuneiform.

23675.q: Roughly how many laws are on Hammurabi's pillar?
23675.e: Researchers count 282 laws. They cover things like trade, family, work and punishments.
23675.m: There are about 280 laws on Hammurabi's pillar.

23676.q: In the picture at the top of the pillar, who is Hammurabi standing in front of?
23676.e: At the top of the pillar you can see the king in front of the sun god Shamash. He was also the god of justice.
23676.m: In the picture, Hammurabi stands in front of the sun god.

23677.q: Roughly how many years ago did King Hammurabi live?
23677.e: Hammurabi reigned from about 1792 to 1750 BC. That is about 3800 years ago.

23678.q: In which modern country was the pillar with Hammurabi's laws found?
23678.e: The pillar was found around 1901 in the ancient city of Susa. An enemy king had once taken it there as loot.
23678.m: The pillar of laws was found in today's Iran.

23679.q: Only ruins remain of the ancient city of Ur today. In which country are they?
23679.e: Ur lies in the south of today's Iraq. It used to be a rich city of the Sumerians.
23679.m: The ruins of Ur are in Iraq.

23680.q: Which river did the city of Ur once lie on?
23680.e: Ur used to lie right on this river. Later the river changed its course, and today it is a few kilometres away.
23680.m: Ur once lay on the Euphrates.

23681.q: What did researchers find in the royal tombs of Ur?
23681.e: The tombs held golden helmets, crowns, necklaces and cups. The finds show how rich the city was.
23681.m: A lot of gold jewellery was found in the royal tombs of Ur.

23682.q: What is the famous box from Ur with pictures of war and peace called?
23682.e: The Standard of Ur is a box with colourful pictures made of shells and blue stone. One side shows war, the other a feast.
23682.m: The Standard of Ur shows pictures of war and peace.

23683.q: When were the royal tombs of Ur excavated?
23683.e: The Englishman Leonard Woolley dug at Ur for many years from 1922. He found the famous royal tombs.
23683.m: The royal tombs of Ur were excavated about 100 years ago.

23684.q: What was found in the tomb of Queen Puabi in Ur?
23684.e: In Puabi's tomb lay a magnificent gold headdress. Her name was on a small seal.
23684.m: The rich tomb of Queen Puabi was found in Ur.

23685.q: What did researchers find in Ur that you can play with?
23685.e: The Royal Game of Ur is a board game with 20 squares. It is one of the oldest board games in the world.
23685.m: One of the oldest board games in the world was found in Ur.

23686.q: Which musical instrument did researchers find in the tombs of Ur?
23686.e: The lyres of Ur are wooden string instruments. Some are decorated with a golden bull's head.
23686.m: Lyres with bulls' heads were found in Ur.

23687.q: Between which two rivers did Mesopotamia lie?
23687.e: Mesopotamia lay between the Euphrates and the Tigris, in the area of today's Iraq. At about 2800 kilometres, the Euphrates is the longer of the two rivers.
23687.m: Mesopotamia lay between the Euphrates and the Tigris.

23688.q: Which country does the Euphrates flow through before it reaches Iraq?
23688.e: The Euphrates comes from the mountains in the north and then flows through Syria. Only after that does it reach Iraq.
23688.m: The Euphrates flows through Syria into Iraq.

23689.q: In which modern country do the Euphrates and Tigris have their source?
23689.e: Both rivers begin in the mountains of eastern Turkey. From there they flow south.
23689.m: The Euphrates and Tigris rise in Turkey.

23690.q: Where do the Euphrates and Tigris flow into in the end?
23690.e: At the end, the two rivers join to form a single river. This flows into the sea in the south.
23690.m: The Euphrates and Tigris flow into the Persian Gulf.

23691.q: Which big capital city lies on the Tigris?
23691.e: Baghdad is the capital of Iraq. The Tigris flows right through the city.

23692.q: What does the name Mesopotamia mean?
23692.e: The name comes from Greek. Mesopotamia lies between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris.
23692.m: Mesopotamia means land between the rivers.

23693.q: Which grain did farmers in Mesopotamia mainly grow?
23693.e: Barley grows even on dry and slightly salty soil. People made bread and beer from it.
23693.m: Barley was the most important grain in Mesopotamia.

23694.q: What did the river floods bring onto the fields?
23694.e: After a flood, nutrient-rich mud was left on the land. Grain grew especially well in it.
23694.m: The rivers' mud made the fields fertile.

23695.q: Which sounds had no signs of their own in the Phoenician alphabet?
23695.e: The Phoenicians only wrote down the consonants. Readers had to add the vowels themselves.
23695.m: The Phoenician alphabet had no signs for vowels.

23696.q: In which direction did the Phoenicians write?
23696.e: The Phoenicians started on the right and wrote towards the left. Hebrew and Arabic, for example, are still written this way today.
23696.m: The Phoenicians wrote from right to left.

23697.q: What was special about the Phoenicians' script?
23697.e: Each sign stood for a sound. So only a few signs were needed, and people could learn to write faster.
23697.m: The Phoenicians wrote with a few signs for sounds.

23698.q: How many letters did the Phoenician alphabet have?
23698.e: The Phoenician alphabet had 22 letters. That is a few fewer than our alphabet with 26 letters.

23699.q: Which people took over the Phoenician alphabet and developed it further?
23699.e: The Greeks added some signs to the alphabet. Our Latin alphabet later developed from their script.
23699.m: The Greeks took over the Phoenician alphabet.

23700.q: Which two letter names make up the word alphabet?
23700.e: Alpha and beta are the first two Greek letters. Together they make the word alphabet.
23700.m: The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta.

23701.q: One of our letters came from the Phoenician sign for an ox. Which one?
23701.e: The sign was called aleph and looked like an ox's head. It became the Greek alpha and our A.
23701.m: Our A comes from the Phoenician sign for an ox.

23702.q: What does the Phoenician sign beth, which became our B, mean?
23702.e: Beth means house. The sign originally looked like a simple floor plan.
23702.m: Our B comes from the Phoenician sign for house.

23703.q: Which Phoenician city does the word Bible indirectly come from?
23703.e: A lot of papyrus was traded through Byblos. So the Greeks gave papyrus and books a name similar to the city, and this became the word Bible.
23703.m: The word Bible goes back to the city of Byblos.

23704.q: What happens to the juice of the purple dye snail in light and air?
23704.e: The juice is almost colourless or yellowish at first. Only in light and air does the precious colour slowly appear.
23704.m: The juice of the purple dye snail changes colour in light and air.

23705.e: Tyrian purple is a strong, dark red with some violet. Depending on how it was made, it was more red or more violet.
23705.m: Tyrian purple is a reddish purple colour.

23706.q: Why was purple dye so expensive?
a: You needed a huge number of snails
Only priests were allowed to dye
23706.e: You needed thousands of snails for a little dye. That is why purple was at times even more expensive than gold.
23706.m: Purple dye was expensive because so many snails were needed.

23707.q: Who wore purple clothes in ancient times?
23707.e: Only very rich and powerful people could afford purple. That is why purple became the colour of rulers.
23707.m: Purple was the colour of kings and emperors.

23708.q: What was especially unpleasant about making purple dye?
23708.e: All the rotting snails smelled awful. That is why the dye works were often outside the cities.

23709.q: Which Phoenician city was especially famous for its purple dye?
23709.e: The purple from Tyre was seen as the best. That is why it was also called Tyrian purple.
23709.m: Tyre was famous for its purple dye.

23710.q: What does the name Phoenicians probably mean?
23710.e: The Greeks gave the people their name. It probably comes from a Greek word for purple-red.
23710.m: The name Phoenicians probably has to do with the colour purple.

23711.q: What did the Phoenicians dye with purple?
23711.e: Wool and cloth were dipped into the dye. Valuable clothes and cloaks were sewn from them.
23711.m: Purple was used to dye cloth and clothes.

23712.q: Which empire built the famous Royal Road?
23712.e: The road linked important cities in a huge empire in what is now Iran and Turkey. It was one of the longest roads of its time.
23712.m: The Royal Road was built in the Persian Empire.

23713.q: Which king had the Persian Royal Road extended?
23713.e: Darius I reigned about 2500 years ago. He wanted news to travel quickly through his empire.
23713.m: Darius I had the Royal Road extended.

23714.q: Roughly how long was the Persian Royal Road?
23714.e: It ran through deserts, valleys and over mountains right across the empire. From Sardis to Susa it was about 2700 kilometres.
23714.m: The Royal Road was about 2700 kilometres long.

23715.q: What was there at regular intervals along the Royal Road?
23715.e: At the stations, messengers could swap their tired horse for a rested one. There were over a hundred such stations.
23715.m: There were stations with fresh horses along the Royal Road.

23716.q: In which modern country did the Persian Royal Road begin in the west?
23716.e: The road began in the city of Sardis in the west of today's Turkey. From there it ran far east to a Persian capital.
23716.m: The Royal Road began in the west of today's Turkey.

23717.q: How long did the mounted messengers need for the whole Royal Road?
23717.e: Because the messengers took turns, someone was always riding a fresh horse. That way they covered the distance in about seven to nine days.
23717.m: The messengers needed only about a week for the Royal Road.

23718.q: How long did a person on foot need for the whole Royal Road?
23718.e: A Greek historian reported about 90 days of walking. That is roughly three months.
23718.m: On foot, the Royal Road took about three months.

23719.q: Which Greek historian described the Persian Royal Road?
23719.e: Herodotus lived about 2500 years ago and wrote a lot about the Persians. He is often called the father of history.
23719.m: Herodotus described the Persian Royal Road.

23720.q: An old saying about the Persian messengers is written on a post office building today. In which city?
23720.e: On the big post office in New York there is a saying which means roughly: neither snow nor rain stops these messengers. It comes from an old account of the Persians.
23720.m: A saying about the Persian messengers is on the post office in New York.

23721.q: In which country are the ruins of Mohenjo-daro today?
23721.e: Mohenjo-daro is in the south of Pakistan. It was one of the largest cities of the Indus civilisation.

23722.e: The city lies close to the Indus. The whole civilisation is named after this river.

23723.q: What is the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro?
a: A river in the middle of the city
23723.e: The pool is about 12 metres long and 7 metres wide and was sealed with bitumen. It may have been used for religious washing.
23723.m: The Great Bath is an ancient brick water pool.

23724.q: What did Mohenjo-daro already have over 4000 years ago?
23724.e: Many houses had a bathroom and a toilet. The dirty water flowed into covered drains under the streets.
23724.m: Mohenjo-daro had drains very early on.

23725.q: How were the streets in Mohenjo-daro laid out?
23725.e: The main streets crossed at right angles, a bit like a grid. So the city was well planned.
23725.m: The streets in Mohenjo-daro were laid out straight and at right angles.

23726.q: Can the script of the Indus civilisation be read today?
a: No, it has not been deciphered
Yes, thanks to a bilingual stone
Yes, it is a kind of cuneiform
23726.e: Many short inscriptions on small seals are known. But so far nobody has been able to decipher the script with certainty.
23726.m: Nobody can read the script of the Indus civilisation yet.

23727.q: Roughly how old is the city of Mohenjo-daro?
23727.e: Mohenjo-daro was built over 4000 years ago. At that time the first great pyramids were also being built in Egypt.

23728.q: What did the people of Mohenjo-daro build their houses from?
23728.e: The houses were made of fired clay bricks. The bricks were all almost the same size.
23728.m: In Mohenjo-daro people built with fired bricks.

23729.q: Which animal with one horn is often shown on seals from Mohenjo-daro?
23729.e: Many small seals show an animal with only one horn. Researchers call it a unicorn, even though it may be a bull seen from the side.
23729.m: Many seals of the Indus civilisation show a unicorn.

23730.q: In which ancient city are the Hanging Gardens said to have stood?
23730.e: The old accounts name Babylon on the Euphrates. But some researchers think the gardens were in another city.
23730.m: The Hanging Gardens are said to have stood in Babylon.

23731.q: What was the Great Wall of China mainly built for?
23731.e: The wall was meant to keep attackers out. Soldiers could guard the land from it.
23731.m: The Great Wall of China was meant to protect the country from enemies.

23732.q: Who did the Chinese want to protect themselves from with the wall?
23732.e: Horse-riding peoples kept coming from the north to attack China. The wall was meant to stop them.
23732.m: The wall protected China from horse-riding peoples from the north.

23733.q: Roughly how long is the Great Wall of China with all its parts?
23733.e: If you add up all the sections of wall from different periods, you get over 20,000 kilometres. That is much longer than the distance from Switzerland to China.
23733.m: With all its parts, the Great Wall of China is over 20,000 kilometres long.

23734.q: What are the parts of the Great Wall that people often visit today made of?
23734.e: The best-known parts were built from stones and fired bricks. The oldest parts were often made of firmly packed earth.
23734.m: The well-known parts of the wall are built of stones and bricks.

23735.q: How did the guards on the Great Wall of China warn of enemies?
23735.e: The guards lit fires on the towers. The smoke and light could be seen very far, from tower to tower.
23735.m: The guards raised the alarm with fire and smoke.

23736.q: Can you see the Great Wall of China from the Moon with the naked eye?
23736.e: The wall is very long, but only a few metres wide. That is why you cannot see it from the Moon.
23736.m: You cannot see the Great Wall of China from the Moon.

23737.q: What are the figures of the Terracotta Army made of?
23737.e: Terracotta means baked earth. The figures were shaped from clay and fired in a kiln.
23737.m: The figures of the Terracotta Army are made of fired clay.

23738.q: What was the Terracotta Army made for?
a: To show children how to fight
23738.e: The clay soldiers were set up by the tomb of a Chinese emperor. They were meant to protect him after his death.
23738.m: The Terracotta Army was meant to protect the dead emperor.

23739.q: Which animals are also part of the Terracotta Army?
23739.e: As well as the soldiers, there are clay horses. Some of them pull chariots.
23739.m: Horses are also part of the Terracotta Army.

23740.q: Who discovered the Terracotta Army in 1974?
23740.e: Farmers wanted to dig a well and came across pieces of clay figures. After that, large excavations began.
23740.m: Farmers found the Terracotta Army while digging a well.

23741.q: Roughly how many figures does the Terracotta Army have?
23741.e: Researchers estimate there are about 8000 soldiers. Many of them have not been dug up yet.
23741.m: The Terracotta Army has about 8000 figures.

23742.q: What do the faces of the clay soldiers look like?
23742.e: The craftsmen gave the soldiers different faces, hairstyles and beards. That is why almost every soldier looks different.
23742.m: Almost every clay soldier has a face of its own.

23743.q: What did the clay soldiers look like originally?
23743.e: The figures were originally painted in colours. Over time the paint has almost completely flaked off.
23743.m: The clay soldiers used to be brightly painted.

23744.q: Who is seen as the inventor of paper in China?
23744.e: Cai Lun was an official at the imperial court. Around AD 105 he improved the way paper was made so much that he is seen as its inventor.
23744.m: Cai Lun is seen as the inventor of paper.

23745.q: What was the first paper in China made from?
a: Plant fibres and scraps of cloth
23745.e: People boiled tree bark, hemp and old scraps of cloth into a pulp. Thin sheets were made from it.
23745.m: The first paper was made from plant fibres and scraps of cloth.

23746.q: What did people in China often write on before there was paper?
23746.e: People wrote on narrow strips of bamboo and tied them together. Such books were very heavy.
23746.m: Before paper, people in China wrote on bamboo.

23747.q: When making paper, what is used to scoop the fibre pulp out of the water?
23747.e: You dip a fine sieve into the fibre pulp and lift it out. The water drains away and a thin layer is left behind.
23747.m: Paper is scooped out of the fibre pulp with a sieve.

23748.q: What is the writing material of the ancient Egyptians, made from a marsh plant, called?
23748.e: Papyrus was made from the stems of a marsh plant. Our word “paper” comes from “papyrus”.
23748.m: The word “paper” comes from Egyptian papyrus.

23749.q: Who brought the art of papermaking from Asia to Europe?
23749.e: The Arabs learned how to make paper and brought it to Europe through Spain. Paper only arrived there in the Middle Ages.
23749.m: The Arabs brought paper to Europe.

23750.q: In which Swiss city is there a museum in an old paper mill?
23750.e: In Basel there is the Basel Paper Mill, a museum of paper, writing and printing. You can make your own paper there.
23750.m: At the Basel Paper Mill you can make paper yourself.

23751.q: Which animal makes the thread for silk?
23751.e: The silkworm spins a very fine thread. The fabric silk is woven from it.

23752.q: Which leaves does the silkworm like to eat most?
23752.e: Silkworms eat almost only the leaves of the mulberry tree. That is why many mulberry trees were planted.

23753.q: What does the silkworm spin around itself?
23753.e: The caterpillar wraps itself in a long thread. This makes a cocoon, from which the silk thread is unwound.
23753.m: The silkworm spins itself into a cocoon.

23754.q: What does a silkworm turn into if you let it hatch?
23754.e: The silkworm turns into a moth called the silk moth. It flies at night.
23754.m: The silkworm turns into a moth.

23755.q: How long can the thread of a single silk cocoon be?
23755.e: A cocoon is made of one single, very long thread. It can be several hundred metres long.
23755.m: A silk cocoon is made of one very long thread.

23756.q: According to a legend, a cocoon fell into a Chinese empress's cup. What was in it?
23756.e: The legend tells of Empress Leizu. In the hot tea the thread came loose from the cocoon, and so she discovered silk.
23756.m: According to the legend, silk was discovered in a cup of tea.

23757.q: For a long time, what was the making of silk in China?
23757.e: Anyone who gave away the secret of silk was severely punished. So only China could make silk and sell it at a high price.
23757.m: For a long time, silk making was a secret in China.

23758.q: Which Swiss city used to be famous for silk fabrics?
23758.e: In Zurich, silk fabrics were woven and traded for many centuries. Zurich's silk industry was once one of the largest in the world.
23758.m: Zurich used to be a famous silk city.

23759.e: The Silk Road was made up of many routes between China and the Mediterranean. Traders carried goods along them from place to place.
23759.m: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes.

23760.q: Between which areas did the Silk Road run?
23760.e: The trade routes ran from China right across Asia to the Mediterranean. There the precious silk was sold on.
23760.m: The Silk Road linked China with the Mediterranean.

23761.q: Which animals carried the goods through the deserts on the Silk Road?
23761.e: Camels can go a long time without water. That made them well suited for travelling through deserts.
23761.m: Camels carried the goods through the deserts.

23762.q: What do you call a group of traders travelling with camels?
23762.e: Traders travelled in caravans, which means in large groups. Together they were safer from robbers.
23762.m: A caravan is a travelling group with camels.

23763.q: Where did traders on the Silk Road stay overnight?
23763.e: A caravanserai was an inn with a courtyard for people and animals. Traders could sleep safely there.
23763.m: In a caravanserai, traders and camels found a place for the night.

23764.q: Did most traders travel the whole way from China to the Mediterranean?
a: No, the goods often changed hands
Yes, they all travelled the whole way
23764.e: Most traders only travelled part of the way. Then they sold the goods on to other traders.
23764.m: On the Silk Road, goods were passed from trader to trader.

23765.q: Apart from goods, what else was passed along the Silk Road?
23765.e: Knowledge, inventions and religions travelled with the traders. That is how Buddhism, for example, came to China.
23765.m: Ideas travelled along the Silk Road too.

23766.q: Which goods did traders from the West like to bring to China?
23766.e: The Chinese valued glass from the West. Silk, tea and paper, on the other hand, were made in China itself.
23766.m: Glassware travelled from the West to China.

23767.e: Qin Shi Huang united several kingdoms into one large empire. He was the first to call himself emperor.
23767.m: Qin Shi Huang was the first emperor of China.

23768.q: In which year did Qin Shi Huang become emperor?
23768.e: By 221 BC he had defeated all his rivals. After that he ruled all of China as emperor.
23768.m: Qin Shi Huang became emperor in 221 BC.

23769.q: What did Qin Shi Huang make the same throughout the empire?
23769.e: Before that, each kingdom had its own written characters, coins and measures. The emperor made them the same everywhere so that the empire held together better.
23769.m: The first emperor made writing, coins and measures the same everywhere.

23770.q: Roughly what does the title “Shi Huangdi” mean?
23770.e: “Shi” means first and “Huangdi” means emperor. He wanted many emperors to come after him.

23771.q: What did Qin Shi Huang search for during his life?
23771.e: The emperor was very afraid of death. He sent people out to find a potion for eternal life.
23771.m: Qin Shi Huang wanted to live for ever.

23772.q: What did Qin Shi Huang have built for the time after his death?
23772.e: While he was still alive he had work begin on a huge tomb. Many thousands of people worked on it.
23772.m: The first emperor had a huge tomb built for himself.

23773.q: What did Qin Shi Huang have burned because he would not tolerate other opinions?
23773.e: The emperor had many books burned that he did not like. Only books about medicine or farming were allowed to stay.
23773.m: The first emperor had many books burned.

23774.q: Which country's name probably comes from the state of Qin?
23774.e: “Qin” is pronounced roughly like “Chin”. Many researchers believe that the name China comes from it.
23774.m: The name China probably comes from the state of Qin.

23775.e: Confucius was a teacher who thought about how people should live together well. His teachings are still known today.
23775.m: Confucius was a famous teacher and thinker.

23776.e: Confucius lived from about 551 to 479 BC. That is about 2500 years ago.

23777.q: What does the Chinese name Kong Fuzi mean?
23777.e: “Fuzi” is a title of honour and means master. “Kong Fuzi” became “Confucius” in the West.

23778.q: What was especially important to Confucius?
a: Respect for parents and older people
23778.e: Confucius taught that children should honour their parents and respect older people. That way families would live together well.
23778.m: For Confucius, respect for parents and older people was very important.

a: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you
The early bird catches the worm
23779.e: Confucius said you should not do anything to others that you would not want yourself. This rule is also known from other religions.
23779.m: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you.

23780.q: Who wrote down the teachings of Confucius?
23780.e: Confucius's pupils wrote down his conversations and sayings. That is how they have survived until today.
23780.m: Confucius's pupils wrote down his teachings.

23781.q: According to Confucius, what should people do all their lives?
23781.e: Confucius thought learning was very important. He believed that people who learn become better people.
23781.m: Confucius said you should keep on learning.

23782.q: By what name is Siddhartha Gautama known?
23782.e: Siddhartha Gautama was later called Buddha. He is the founder of a major religion.
23782.m: Siddhartha Gautama is known as Buddha.

23783.e: Buddha means the awakened one. After a long search, Siddhartha had gained an important insight about life.

23784.q: What was Siddhartha Gautama before he became Buddha?
23784.e: Siddhartha was the son of a ruler and lived in a palace. There he had everything he wanted.
23784.m: Siddhartha Gautama was a prince at first.

23785.q: In which modern country was Siddhartha Gautama born?
23785.e: He was born in Lumbini. This place is in Nepal today, near the border with India.
23785.m: Buddha was born in today's Nepal.

23786.q: What did the young prince see for the first time outside the palace?
23786.e: In the palace, suffering had been kept away from him. Outside he saw old, sick and dead people and became very thoughtful.
23786.m: Outside, Siddhartha saw old age and illness for the first time.

23787.q: Under what kind of tree did Siddhartha awaken?
23787.e: The tree was a sacred fig. It is also called the Bodhi tree, which means tree of awakening.
23787.m: Buddha awakened under a fig tree.

23788.q: Which religion goes back to Siddhartha Gautama?
23788.e: Buddhism grew out of his teachings. Today Buddhists live all over the world, including in Switzerland.
23788.m: Buddhism goes back to Siddhartha Gautama.

23789.q: What are the famous colossal heads of the Olmecs?
23789.e: The Olmecs carved huge heads out of stone. Some are almost three metres high.
23789.m: The Olmecs made huge stone heads.

23790.q: In which modern country were the Olmec heads found?
23790.e: The Olmecs lived on the coast of the Gulf of Mexico. Their stone heads were found there.
23790.m: The Olmec heads come from Mexico.

23791.q: Roughly how big are the largest Olmec heads?
a: As tall as a church tower
23791.e: The largest stone heads are almost three metres high. That is taller than a room.
23791.m: The largest Olmec heads are almost three metres high.

23792.q: How heavy is a large Olmec head?
23792.e: The largest heads weigh many tonnes, as much as several cars put together. You cannot simply lift them.
23792.m: An Olmec head weighs several tonnes.

23793.q: Which rock are the Olmec heads carved from?
23793.e: The heads are made of basalt, a hard rock from volcanoes. The blocks came from mountains far away.
23793.m: The Olmec heads are made of volcanic rock.

23794.q: Who do the Olmec heads probably show?
23794.e: Researchers believe the heads show important rulers. Each head has its own facial features.
23794.m: The Olmec heads probably show rulers.

23795.q: Roughly how old are the Olmec heads?
23795.e: The Olmecs lived about 3000 years ago. They are one of the oldest advanced civilisations in the Americas.
23795.m: The Olmec heads are about 3000 years old.

23796.q: Roughly what does the name “Olmecs” mean?
23796.e: Rubber trees grew in their region. Rubber can be made from their sap.
23796.m: Olmecs means people from the rubber land.

23797.q: What shape are the pyramids of the Maya?
23797.e: Maya pyramids are step pyramids. A steep staircase leads to the top.

23798.q: What often stood at the very top of a Maya pyramid?
23798.e: A small temple stood at the top. Priests held ceremonies for the gods there.
23798.m: A temple often stood on top of Maya pyramids.

23799.q: What is the name of a famous Maya city with a large pyramid?
23799.e: Chichén Itzá is in Mexico. Machu Picchu, on the other hand, was built by the Incas in Peru.
23799.m: Chichén Itzá is a famous Maya city.

23800.q: In which part of the world did the Maya build their pyramids?
23800.e: The Maya lived in what is now Mexico, Guatemala and neighbouring countries. This region is called Central America.
23800.m: The Maya built their pyramids in Central America.

23801.q: The pyramid of Chichén Itzá has 4 staircases with 91 steps each and one more step at the top. How many steps is that?
23801.e: 4 times 91 is 364, and with the top step it makes 365. That is how many days a year has.
23801.m: The pyramid of Chichén Itzá has as many steps as the year has days.

23802.q: What can you see on the pyramid of Chichén Itzá in spring and autumn?
23802.e: On two days a year, the sun casts shadows on the staircase. It looks as if a snake is crawling down the pyramid.
23802.m: A shadow snake appears on the pyramid of Chichén Itzá.

23803.q: Where are many old Maya pyramids today?
23803.e: Many Maya cities were overgrown by the rainforest. Some pyramids are still being discovered in the jungle today.
23803.m: Many Maya pyramids are in the rainforest.

23804.q: Which game did the Maya play on courts next to their pyramids?
23804.e: The Maya built ball courts with high walls. The heavy rubber ball was not allowed to be touched with the hands.
23804.m: The Maya played a ball game on special courts.

23805.q: What value does a dot have in the Maya number system?
23805.e: The Maya wrote one as a dot. Two dots mean 2.
23805.m: For the Maya, a dot means one.

23806.q: What value does a bar have in the Maya number system?
23806.e: For the Maya, a horizontal bar means 5. It replaces five dots.
23806.m: For the Maya, a bar means five.

23807.q: How did the Maya write zero?
23807.e: For zero the Maya drew a sign that looks like a shell. Many other peoples did not yet know zero at that time.
23807.m: The Maya wrote zero as a shell.

23808.q: What number do three dots mean for the Maya?
23808.e: Each dot counts as 1. So three dots are 1 plus 1 plus 1, which makes 3.
23808.m: For the Maya, three dots mean three.

23809.q: For the Maya, a bar is 5 and a dot is 1. What number are two bars and one dot?
23809.e: Each bar is 5 and the dot is 1. So 5 plus 5 plus 1 makes 11.
23809.m: For the Maya, two bars and one dot make eleven.

23810.q: For the Maya, a bar is 5. What number are three bars?
23810.e: Each bar is 5. Three bars are 5 plus 5 plus 5, which makes 15.
23810.m: For the Maya, three bars mean fifteen.

23811.q: The Maya wrote a bar instead of five dots. So what is the most dots that can stand side by side?
23811.e: You do not write five dots, because there is a bar for that. So at most 4 dots stand side by side.
23811.m: With the Maya, at most four dots stand side by side.

23812.q: The Maya counted in groups of twenty. What is this probably connected with?
23812.e: A person has 10 fingers and 10 toes, 20 altogether. That made counting easy.
23812.m: The Maya probably counted to twenty with fingers and toes.

23813.q: How many days did the Maya solar year have?
23813.e: The Maya solar year is called the Haab. It had 365 days, almost like our year.
23813.m: The Maya solar year had 365 days.

23814.q: How many days did a month have in the Maya solar year?
23814.e: In the Maya solar year, each month had exactly 20 days. This fits their way of counting in twenties.
23814.m: A Maya month lasted twenty days.

23815.q: A Maya year had 18 months of 20 days each. How many days is that?
23815.e: 18 times 20 is 360 days. A few extra days were added at the end of the year.
23815.m: Eighteen months of twenty days each make 360 days.
