24195.m: Marcus Aurelius was a philosopher on the imperial throne.

24196.q: What did Marcus Aurelius write down for himself?
24196.e: Marcus Aurelius wrote his thoughts down in a book. It is called the “Meditations” and is still read today.

24197.q: In which language did Marcus Aurelius write his “Meditations”?
24197.e: Although he was a Roman, Marcus Aurelius wrote in Greek. At that time Greek was the language of scholars.
24197.m: Marcus Aurelius wrote his thoughts in Greek.

24198.q: How does the famous bronze statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome show the emperor?
24198.e: The equestrian statue shows Marcus Aurelius on his horse. Today the original is in the museum on the Capitoline Hill.
24198.m: A famous statue shows Marcus Aurelius on horseback.

24199.q: Why was the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius not melted down?
24199.e: Many bronze statues were later melted down. This one survived because people believed it showed Emperor Constantine.
24199.m: The statue of Marcus Aurelius survived thanks to a mix-up.

24200.q: On which great river did Marcus Aurelius wage war for a long time against Germanic peoples?
24200.e: On the Danube, Marcus Aurelius fought the Marcomanni and other tribes. He spent many years there.
24200.m: Marcus Aurelius fought for a long time on the Danube.

24201.q: Who became emperor after Marcus Aurelius?
24201.e: After the death of Marcus Aurelius in AD 180, his son Commodus became emperor. Commodus was very different from his father.
24201.m: Commodus succeeded his father Marcus Aurelius.

24202.q: What does the Latin word “testudo” mean?
24202.e: “Testudo” means tortoise. The formation is reminiscent of a tortoise’s hard shell.
24202.m: Testudo is the Latin word for tortoise.

24203.q: Roman soldiers stood close together and then looked like a tortoise. What did they make the shell with?
24203.e: The soldiers held their shields in front of them, beside them and over their heads. This made a shell of shields.
24203.m: In the tortoise, shields form a shell.

24204.q: What did the tortoise formation mainly protect the soldiers from?
24204.e: The shields above their heads kept off arrows, spears and stones. The soldiers underneath stayed protected.
24204.m: The tortoise protected against arrows and stones.

24205.q: Where did the soldiers in the middle of the tortoise hold their shields?
24205.e: The soldiers on the outside held their shields to the side and to the front. The soldiers inside held them like a roof over their heads.
24205.m: In the middle of the tortoise, shields form a roof.

24206.q: How did a tortoise formation move forward?
a: At a run in a wide line
24206.e: All the soldiers had to stay close together so that the shields closed without gaps. That is why the formation moved only slowly.
24206.m: The tortoise moved slowly and tightly packed.

24207.q: When did the Romans like to use the tortoise formation?
a: In horse races in the circus
24207.e: Enemies on the walls shot arrows and threw stones. Under the shields the soldiers could reach the wall safely.
24207.m: The tortoise helped when attacking city walls.

24208.q: What were the Roman foot soldiers who formed the tortoise called?
24208.e: The foot soldiers of the Roman army were called legionaries. They were well trained and often practised the tortoise.
24208.m: Roman foot soldiers were called legionaries.

24209.q: What did the soldiers have to practise a lot for a good tortoise?
24209.e: Only if all the soldiers walked at exactly the same speed did the shields stay close together. Otherwise gaps appeared.
24209.m: For the tortoise everyone had to march in step.

24210.e: The denarius was a coin the Romans paid with. For a long time it was the most important coin in the empire.
24210.m: The denarius was a Roman coin.

24211.q: What metal was the denarius made of?
24211.e: The denarius was a silver coin. Later the Romans mixed in more and more cheaper metal.
24211.m: The denarius was a silver coin.

24212.q: Whose head could often be seen on Roman coins?
24212.e: The emperors had their faces stamped on the coins. That way everyone in the empire knew their ruler.
24212.m: You often see the emperor on Roman coins.

24213.q: What does the Latin word “denarius” mean?
24213.e: At first a denarius was worth 10 small coins called asses. That is why its name means “containing ten”.

24214.q: What was the Roman gold coin called?
24214.e: The aureus was made of gold and worth much more than a denarius. “Aurum” is Latin for gold.
24214.m: The Roman gold coin was called the aureus.

24215.q: Which was worth more for the Romans, a denarius or a sestertius?
24215.e: A sestertius was worth only a quarter of a denarius. Four sestertii made one denarius.
24215.m: A denarius was worth more than a sestertius.

24216.q: Which Roman town near Basel has produced many coin finds?
24216.e: Augusta Raurica is at Augst and Kaiseraugst near Basel. Many coins and a large silver treasure were found there.
24216.m: Many Roman coins were found at Augusta Raurica.

24217.q: Which currency still has a name that comes from the denarius?
24217.e: The dinar is the currency of Serbia, for example. Its name comes from the Roman denarius.
24217.m: The name dinar comes from the Roman denarius.

24218.q: What does the saying “All roads lead to Rome” mean?
a: There are many ways to reach a goal
You must always travel to Rome
There is only one right way
24218.e: The saying means you can reach a goal in different ways. There is not just one right way.
24218.m: All roads lead to Rome means there are many ways to reach a goal.

24219.q: Why did many roads in the Roman Empire lead to Rome?
a: Rome was in the middle of the Alps
Rome was by the North Sea
24219.e: Rome was the capital of the great empire. The Romans built roads from Rome to all the provinces.
24219.m: The Romans built roads from their capital in all directions.

24220.q: What was the top layer of important Roman roads made of?
24220.e: Important Roman roads had large, smooth stone slabs on top. Carts could travel well on them.
24220.m: Roman roads were often paved with stone slabs.

24221.q: What does the Latin word “via” mean?
24221.e: “Via” means way or road in Latin. That is why many Roman roads have the word “Via” in their name.
24221.m: Via is the Latin word for road.

24222.q: How many double steps were there in a Roman mile?
24222.e: Mile comes from the Latin “mille”, which means thousand. A Roman mile had 1000 double steps, which is about 1.5 kilometres.
24222.m: A Roman mile had a thousand double steps.

24223.q: What is the saying “All roads lead to Rome” in French?
a: Tous les chemins mènent à Rome
Toutes les routes sont à Paris
24223.e: The saying exists in many languages. In French it is “Tous les chemins mènent à Rome”.
24223.m: In French too, all roads lead to Rome.

24224.q: Who usually built the roads in the Roman Empire?
24224.e: Soldiers did not only work in war. In peaceful times they built roads, bridges and camps.

24225.q: Which other well-known saying is also about Rome?
a: Rome wasn’t built in a day
Rome was built in one night
24225.e: This saying means that great things take time. So you should be patient.
24225.m: Rome wasn’t built in a day means great things take time.

24226.q: How many wonders of the world were counted in ancient times?
24226.e: Greek writers put together a list of seven especially amazing buildings. We still know this list today.
24226.m: The ancient world had seven wonders.

24227.q: What stone is the Pyramid of Khufu mainly made of?
24227.e: Most of the pyramid is made of limestone blocks. It also used to be covered with pale, smooth limestone slabs.
24227.m: The Pyramid of Khufu is mainly built of limestone.

24228.q: What was the Pyramid of Khufu built for?
a: As a tomb for a pharaoh
24228.e: The pyramid was the tomb of Pharaoh Khufu. It was built about 4500 years ago.
24228.m: The Pyramid of Khufu is the tomb of a pharaoh.

24229.q: Which is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the World?
24229.e: The Pyramid of Khufu is about 2000 years older than the other wonders. It was built about 4500 years ago.
24229.m: The Pyramid of Khufu is the oldest wonder of the world.

24230.q: In which ancient city are the Hanging Gardens said to have been?
24230.e: The Hanging Gardens are said to have been in Babylon in present-day Iraq. Babylon lay on the River Euphrates.
24230.m: The Hanging Gardens are said to have stood in Babylon.

24231.q: Which king is said to have created the Hanging Gardens of Babylon?
24231.e: A legend says that Nebuchadnezzar II had the gardens made for his wife. She is said to have been homesick for green mountains.
24231.m: The Hanging Gardens are credited to King Nebuchadnezzar II.

24232.q: Which wonder of the world is it still unclear really existed?
24232.e: No clear remains of the Hanging Gardens have been found so far. That is why some researchers doubt that they existed.
24232.m: Nobody knows for sure whether the Hanging Gardens really existed.

24233.q: Who did the Colossus of Rhodes show?
a: Zeus, the father of the gods
24233.e: Helios was the protector god of the island of Rhodes. The people built the huge statue in his honour.
24233.m: The Colossus of Rhodes showed the sun god Helios.

24234.q: What metal was the Colossus of Rhodes made of?
24234.e: The statue was made of cast bronze. Inside, iron bars and stones probably held it up.
24234.m: The Colossus of Rhodes was made of bronze.

24235.q: Roughly how tall was the Colossus of Rhodes?
24235.e: The Colossus was about 30 metres tall. That is as high as a building with ten storeys.
24235.m: The Colossus of Rhodes was about 30 metres tall.

24236.q: Where is the island of Rhodes today?
24236.e: Rhodes is a Greek island in the Mediterranean. It lies close to the coast of Turkey.
24236.m: The island of Rhodes belongs to Greece.

24237.q: What destroyed the Colossus of Rhodes?
24237.e: A strong earthquake made the statue fall over. Afterwards it lay on the ground in pieces for a long time.
24237.m: An earthquake brought down the Colossus of Rhodes.

24238.q: Which wonder of the world stood for the shortest time?
24238.e: The Colossus only stood for about 60 years. The other wonders stood for many centuries.
24238.m: The Colossus of Rhodes only stood for a few decades.

24239.q: How did the people of Rhodes pay for the Colossus?
24239.e: An enemy had besieged the city and then withdrawn. The siege machines he left behind were sold to pay for the statue.
24239.m: Selling war equipment paid for the Colossus of Rhodes.

24240.q: Which well-known story about the Colossus is probably not true?
a: It stood astride the harbour entrance
It fell over in an earthquake
24240.e: In many pictures the Colossus stands with its legs apart over the harbour. That would hardly have been technically possible and is seen as a legend.
24240.m: That the Colossus stood over the harbour is just a legend.

24241.q: On which island did the Lighthouse of Alexandria stand?
24241.e: The lighthouse stood on the small island of Pharos in front of the harbour. That is why it is often simply called “the Pharos”.
24241.m: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on the island of Pharos.

24242.q: In which present-day country is Alexandria?
24242.e: Alexandria is a large port city in Egypt on the Mediterranean. It was founded by Alexander the Great.

24243.q: Who is the city of Alexandria named after?
24243.e: Alexander the Great founded the city in 331 BC. It still bears his name today.
24243.m: Alexandria bears the name of Alexander the Great.

24244.q: What was the Lighthouse of Alexandria for?
24244.e: At the top a fire burnt that could be seen far out to sea. That way ships found their way safely into the harbour.
24244.m: The lighthouse showed ships the way into the harbour.

24245.q: Roughly how tall was the Lighthouse of Alexandria?
24245.e: It is estimated that the tower was over 100 metres tall. That made it one of the tallest buildings of its time.
24245.m: The Lighthouse of Alexandria was over 100 metres tall.

24246.q: What does the French word “phare” mean?
24246.e: The word recalls the famous lighthouse of Alexandria. In Italian, too, a lighthouse is called “faro”.
24246.m: The island of Pharos gave the lighthouse its French name.

24247.q: What destroyed the Lighthouse of Alexandria?
24247.e: In the Middle Ages several earthquakes badly damaged the tower. In the end only ruins were left.
24247.m: Earthquakes destroyed the Lighthouse of Alexandria.

24248.q: What was later built from the stones of the lighthouse?
24248.e: A sultan had the Citadel of Qaitbay built on the same spot. Stones from the old tower were used for it.
24248.m: A fortress was built from the stones of the lighthouse.

24249.q: Who created the Statue of Zeus at Olympia?
24249.e: Phidias was one of the most famous sculptors in Greece. He created the statue around 430 BC.
24249.m: The sculptor Phidias created the Statue of Zeus.

24250.q: On which Greek peninsula is Olympia?
24250.e: Olympia is in the west of the Peloponnese peninsula in Greece. The famous Statue of Zeus once stood there.
24250.m: Olympia is on the Peloponnese peninsula.

24251.q: How was Zeus shown in the statue at Olympia?
24251.e: Zeus sat on a magnificent throne. If he had stood up, he would have gone through the roof of the temple.
24251.m: The Statue of Zeus showed the god sitting on a throne.

24252.q: Which precious materials decorated the Statue of Zeus?
24252.e: The skin was made of ivory, the robe of gold. Underneath there was a wooden frame.
24252.m: The Statue of Zeus gleamed with gold and ivory.

24253.q: Roughly how tall was the Statue of Zeus?
24253.e: The seated figure was about 12 metres tall. It filled the temple almost up to the ceiling.
24253.m: The Statue of Zeus was about 12 metres tall.

24254.q: What was Olympia famous for in ancient times?
24254.e: Every four years, sports contests were held at Olympia in honour of Zeus. Today’s Olympic Games are named after them.
24254.m: Olympia was the home of the ancient Olympic Games.

24255.q: In which building did the Statue of Zeus stand?
a: In the Temple of Zeus at Olympia
24255.e: A large temple was built at Olympia for the statue. Today only ruins of it can be seen.
24255.m: The Statue of Zeus stood in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia.

24256.q: What did researchers find at Olympia that belongs to the Statue of Zeus?
24256.e: Archaeologists discovered the sculptor’s workshop with tools and moulds. The statue itself is lost.
24256.m: At Olympia the workshop of the sculptor of the Statue of Zeus was found.

24257.q: Which goddess was the temple at Ephesus dedicated to?
24257.e: The huge temple belonged to the goddess Artemis. That is why it was also called the Artemision.
24257.m: The temple at Ephesus was dedicated to the goddess Artemis.

24258.q: What was the goddess Artemis responsible for?
24258.e: Artemis was the goddess of hunting and wild animals. She is often shown with a bow and arrows.
24258.m: Artemis was the goddess of hunting.

24259.q: In which present-day country is Ephesus?
24259.e: The ruins of Ephesus are on the west coast of present-day Turkey. In the past there was a rich Greek city there.

24260.q: What happened to the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus in 356 BC?
a: A man set fire to it to become famous
An earthquake made it sink into the sea
The Romans turned it into a theatre
It was taken to Athens stone by stone
24260.e: A man called Herostratus started a fire because he wanted to become famous at any cost. The temple burnt down and was later rebuilt.
24260.m: Herostratus set fire to the Temple of Artemis to become famous.

24261.q: What destroyed the Temple of Artemis in 356 BC?
24261.e: A man called Herostratus set fire to the temple because he wanted to become famous. Later the temple was rebuilt.
24261.m: The Temple of Artemis was destroyed by fire.

24262.q: What can still be seen of the Temple of Artemis today?
24262.e: Of the more than a hundred columns, only one, which has been put back up, stands today. The rest lies in ruins.
24262.m: Only one column of the Temple of Artemis stands today.

24263.q: What stone was the Temple of Artemis built from?
24263.e: The temple was one of the first large buildings made entirely of marble. That made it especially splendid.
24263.m: The Temple of Artemis was built of marble.

24264.q: Which rich king helped build the first great Temple of Artemis?
24264.e: King Croesus of Lydia was famous for his wealth. He donated columns for the temple.
24264.m: The rich King Croesus helped build the Temple of Artemis.

24265.q: Who was the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus built for?
24265.e: The Mausoleum was the tomb of King Mausolus. He died in 353 BC.
24265.m: The Mausoleum was the tomb of King Mausolus.

24266.q: What was the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus?
24266.e: The dead king lay in this splendid building. It was a huge, decorated tomb.
24266.m: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was a tomb.

24267.q: What does the word “mausoleum” mean today?
24267.e: Because the tomb of Mausolus was so famous, splendid tomb buildings are called mausoleums today. The word comes from the king’s name.
24267.m: A mausoleum is a large tomb.

24268.q: What stood right at the top of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus?
24268.e: On the top of the tomb stood a stone chariot with four horses. Parts of it can be seen in a museum today.
24268.m: A chariot with four horses stood on top of the Mausoleum.

24269.q: What is the city of Halicarnassus called today?
24269.e: Halicarnassus is today’s town of Bodrum. It lies on the coast of Turkey.

24270.q: Roughly how tall was the Mausoleum?
24270.e: The tomb was about 45 metres tall. At the top stood a stone chariot with four horses.
24270.m: The Mausoleum was about 45 metres tall.

24271.q: What did knights later use many stones from the Mausoleum for?
24271.e: The Knights of St John built a castle in Bodrum. For it they took stones from the crumbling Mausoleum.
24271.m: Knights built a castle with stones from the Mausoleum.

24272.q: In which museum are many figures from the Mausoleum today?
a: The Swiss National Museum in Zurich
24272.e: In the 19th century researchers brought statues and reliefs to England. Today they are on display in the British Museum.
24272.m: Many figures from the Mausoleum are in the British Museum in London.

24273.q: In which city was the most famous library of the ancient world?
24273.e: The Library of Alexandria was the largest collection of books in the ancient world. It stood in Egypt.
24273.m: The most famous library of the ancient world was in Alexandria.

24274.q: What were the texts in the Library of Alexandria written on?
24274.e: The texts were on long scrolls of papyrus. Books with pages like today did not exist yet.
24274.m: In Alexandria the texts were on papyrus scrolls.

24275.e: Papyrus is a plant that grows by the Nile. Sheets for writing on were made from its stems.
24275.m: Papyrus is made from a plant from the Nile.

24276.q: In which country was the Library of Alexandria?
24276.e: Alexandria is in Egypt on the Mediterranean. Greek kings founded the library there more than 2000 years ago.
24276.m: The Library of Alexandria was in Egypt.

24277.q: What happened to books on ships that came to Alexandria?
24277.e: Books on arriving ships were taken and copied. The library often kept the original and gave back a copy.
24277.m: Alexandria had books from ships copied.

24278.q: Which scholar from the library calculated the circumference of the Earth?
24278.e: Eratosthenes ran the library. He measured shadows in two places and from this calculated the Earth’s circumference quite accurately.
24278.m: Eratosthenes calculated the circumference of the Earth in Alexandria.

24279.q: Does the old Library of Alexandria still exist today?
a: Yes, it is still completely standing
Yes, about half of it still stands
No, but all the scrolls survive
24279.e: The library was gradually destroyed by fires and wars. None of the scrolls have survived.
24279.m: The old Library of Alexandria is lost.

24280.e: The Bibliotheca Alexandrina recalls the famous old library. It is a modern library with room for millions of books.
24280.m: Since 2002 Alexandria has had a large library again.

24281.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Carthage?
24281.e: Carthage lay on the Mediterranean. Today the ruins are near the capital, Tunis.

24282.q: Which people founded the city of Carthage?
24282.e: Seafarers from Phoenicia founded Carthage on the coast of North Africa. From there they traded across the whole Mediterranean.

24283.q: According to legend, which queen founded Carthage?
24283.e: The legend tells of Queen Dido, who fled from her homeland. She founded Carthage on a foreign coast.
24283.m: According to legend, Queen Dido founded Carthage.

24284.q: Who won the wars between Rome and Carthage in the end?
24284.e: After three wars Rome won. In 146 BC the Romans destroyed Carthage.
24284.m: In the end Rome defeated Carthage.

24285.q: What are the wars between Rome and Carthage called?
24285.e: The Romans called the Carthaginians “Punici”. That is why the wars are called the Punic Wars.
24285.m: The wars between Rome and Carthage are called the Punic Wars.

24286.q: Which general from Carthage crossed the Alps with elephants?
24286.e: In 218 BC Hannibal crossed the Alps with his army and war elephants. He wanted to attack Rome from the north.
24286.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants.

24287.e: Carthage was on the north coast of Africa. From there it was not far to Sicily.

24288.q: In which year did the Romans destroy Carthage?
24288.e: At the end of the Third Punic War the Romans captured the city and destroyed it. Later they built a Roman city there.

24289.q: How did the Carthaginians mainly make their living?
a: From raising livestock in the mountains
24289.e: Carthage had a large harbour and many ships. The traders carried goods across the whole Mediterranean.
24289.m: Carthage grew rich through trade across the sea.

24290.q: On which island is the palace of Knossos?
24290.e: Knossos is on Crete, the largest island in Greece. The Minoans lived there.
24290.m: The palace of Knossos is on Crete.

24291.q: Which legendary king is the culture of Knossos named after?
24291.e: The culture on Crete is called the Minoan culture. The name comes from the legendary King Minos.
24291.m: The Minoan culture is named after King Minos.

24292.q: According to legend, who built the labyrinth for King Minos?
24292.e: Daedalus was a brilliant inventor and builder. Later he escaped from Crete with his son Icarus on wings.
24292.m: The inventor Daedalus built the labyrinth.

24293.q: What is special about the red columns in the palace of Knossos?
a: They get narrower towards the bottom
They get narrower towards the top
They are twisted like a rope
24293.e: The red wooden columns are wider at the top than at the bottom. That is exactly the opposite of Greek temples.
24293.m: The columns at Knossos get narrower towards the bottom.

24294.q: Roughly how old are the remains of the palace of Knossos?
24294.e: The palace was built in the Bronze Age and rebuilt several times. It was at its height about 3500 years ago.
24294.m: The palace of Knossos is about 3500 years old.

24295.q: What helped Theseus find his way out of the labyrinth?
24295.e: The king’s daughter gave him a thread. He unwound it and followed it back to the exit.
24295.m: Theseus found his way out of the labyrinth with a thread.

24296.q: Apart from excavating, what did the Englishman Arthur Evans do at Knossos?
a: He rebuilt parts of the palace
He built a hotel in the ruins
He took the whole palace to London
24296.e: Evans excavated the palace from 1900. He had some parts rebuilt with concrete and painted, which is controversial today.
24296.m: Arthur Evans rebuilt parts of Knossos.

24297.q: Which animal can be seen in many pictures at Knossos?
24297.e: In wall paintings young people leap over bulls. The bull was an important animal on Crete.
24297.m: The bull can be seen in many pictures at Knossos.

24298.q: In which present-day country did the Etruscans live?
24298.e: The Etruscans lived in central Italy. They were at their height before Rome became powerful.
24298.m: The Etruscans lived in present-day Italy.

24299.q: Which present-day region of Italy is named after the Etruscans?
24299.e: The Romans also called the Etruscans “Tusci”. The name Tuscany comes from this.
24299.m: Tuscany is named after the Etruscans.

24300.q: Which city was ruled by Etruscan kings in its early days?
24300.e: The last kings of Rome were Etruscans. After the last king, Rome became a republic.
24300.m: In its early days Rome was ruled by Etruscan kings.

24301.q: What did the Etruscans often decorate with paintings?
24301.e: The Etruscans built burial chambers like small houses. The walls are painted with cheerful pictures of feasts and dances.
24301.m: The Etruscans painted pictures in their tombs.

24302.q: What is special about the language of the Etruscans?
a: It is still not fully understood today
It is the same as Latin
24302.e: Etruscan writing can be read because it is similar to the Greek alphabet. But many words are still not understood today.
24302.m: The Etruscan language has still not been fully deciphered.

24303.q: Which people in the Alps probably had a language related to Etruscan?
24303.e: The Raetians lived in places including what is now the Grisons. Their language was probably related to Etruscan.
24303.m: The Raetian language was probably related to the Etruscan language.

24304.q: What were the Etruscans especially skilled at?
24304.e: The Etruscans made artistic figures, mirrors and vessels from bronze. A famous example is the Chimera of Arezzo.
24304.m: The Etruscans were skilled bronze casters.

24305.q: What did Etruscan priests examine to predict the future?
24305.e: The priests read the will of the gods from the livers of sacrificed animals. A bronze model of such a liver was found near Piacenza.
24305.m: Etruscan priests read the future from animals’ livers.

24306.q: Which people took over a lot from the Etruscans?
24306.e: The Romans lived right next to the Etruscans. They took over religious customs and symbols of power, for example.
24306.m: The Romans took over a lot from the Etruscans.

24307.q: Which people built the rock city of Petra?
24307.e: The Nabataeans were a trading people from Arabia. Petra was their capital.
24307.m: The Nabataeans built the rock city of Petra.

24308.q: How were the buildings of Petra built?
a: They were carved into the rock
They were built of mud bricks
They were built of marble blocks
24308.e: The facades were chiselled straight out of the rock walls. That is why Petra is called a rock city.
24308.m: In Petra the buildings were carved into the rock.

24309.q: What colour is the rock of Petra?
24309.e: Petra is carved from reddish sandstone. That is why it is also called the “rose-red city”.
24309.m: The rock of Petra glows reddish.

24310.q: What is the most famous building in Petra called?
24310.e: In Arabic the Treasury is called Khazne al-Firaun. A legend told of a treasure in the urn at the top of the facade.
24310.m: The Treasury of the Pharaoh is the most famous building in Petra.

24311.q: How do you get into the city of Petra on foot?
24311.e: The way leads through the Siq, a narrow rocky gorge. At the end you suddenly see the Treasury.
24311.m: A narrow gorge leads into the rock city of Petra.

24312.q: Which Swiss city did the explorer come from who discovered Petra for Europe in 1812?
24312.e: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt came from a Basel family and grew up in Basel. He travelled through the region in disguise and in 1812 became the first European in a long time to see Petra.
24312.m: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt from Basel discovered Petra for Europe.

24313.q: Which list was Petra voted onto in 2007?
a: The New Seven Wonders of the World
24313.e: In a worldwide vote in 2007, Petra became one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. It has also been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.
24313.m: Since 2007 Petra has been one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

24314.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Troy?
24314.e: Troy lies on a hill in north-west Turkey. The hill is called Hisarlik.
24314.m: The ruins of Troy are in Turkey.

24315.q: Which poet told of the war over Troy?
24315.e: The Greek poet Homer described the war in a long poem. The work is almost 3000 years old.
24315.m: Homer told of the war over Troy.

24316.q: What is Homer’s work about the war over Troy called?
24316.e: The Iliad tells of part of the war over Troy. The name comes from “Ilion”, another name for Troy.
24316.m: Homer’s work about Troy is called the Iliad.

24317.q: Who was Paris in the legend of Troy?
24317.e: Paris was a son of the king of Troy. He carried off a queen from Greece and so started the war.
24317.m: Paris was a prince of Troy.

24318.q: What did researchers find in the hill of Troy?
a: Many cities on top of each other
24318.e: The remains of many settlements lie on top of each other in the hill. Again and again, people built anew on the ruins.
24318.m: Many cities lie on top of each other in the hill of Troy.

24319.q: What did Heinrich Schliemann want to find?
24319.e: Schliemann believed that Homer’s stories were true. So he searched for the city from the legend.
24319.m: Heinrich Schliemann searched for the city of Troy.

24320.q: Which country did Heinrich Schliemann come from?
24320.e: Schliemann was born in 1822 in Mecklenburg in Germany. He became very rich as a merchant.

24321.q: How did Heinrich Schliemann first earn his money?
24321.e: Schliemann became rich through trading. He later used this money to pay for his excavations.
24321.m: Schliemann became rich as a merchant.

24322.q: What did Schliemann find at Troy in 1873?
24322.e: Schliemann called the find “Priam’s Treasure”, after the king of Troy. Later it turned out that the treasure is much older.
24322.m: Schliemann found a gold treasure at Troy.

24323.q: Where did Schliemann find a famous golden death mask?
24323.e: At Mycenae in Greece, Schliemann excavated royal tombs. He called one gold mask the “Mask of Agamemnon”.
24323.m: Schliemann found a golden death mask at Mycenae.

24324.q: Which site on Lake Neuchâtel is a period of the Celts named after?
24324.e: At La Tène near Marin, a great many Celtic weapons and pieces of jewellery were found. That is why the late Celtic period is called the La Tène period.
24324.m: A period of the Celts is named after La Tène.

24325.q: Where did the Helvetii mainly live?
24325.e: The Helvetii lived mainly in the Plateau between the Jura and the Alps. There was good land for fields and livestock there.
24325.m: The Helvetii lived mainly in the Plateau.

24326.e: An oppidum was a large settlement with walls or ramparts. The Celts often built them on hills or by rivers.
24326.m: An oppidum was a protected Celtic settlement.

24327.q: Which Roman general defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte?
24327.e: In 58 BC Caesar defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte in Gaul. After that they had to return to their homeland.
24327.m: Caesar defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte.

24328.q: Which river flows around the peninsula in Bern where the Helvetii had a large settlement?
24328.e: In Bern the Aare forms several loops. On the Enge peninsula there was a fortified settlement of the Helvetii, and later a small Roman settlement too.
24328.m: In Bern the Helvetii settled in a loop of the Aare.

24329.q: What did the Helvetii want to do in 58 BC?
a: Build a wall around the Alps
24329.e: The Helvetii burnt their villages and wanted to look for new land to the west in Gaul. Caesar stopped them.
24329.m: In 58 BC the Helvetii wanted to emigrate to Gaul.

24330.q: What was the name of a famous leader of the Helvetii?
24330.e: Divico led the Helvetii against the Romans. Even as a young man he had defeated a Roman army.
24330.m: Divico was a leader of the Helvetii.

24331.q: What did the Helvetii pay with when trading?
24331.e: The Helvetii had their own metal coins. In 1890 a large lump made of such coins was even found in Zurich.

24332.q: In which year did the Helvetii leave their homeland?
24332.e: In 58 BC the Helvetii set off westwards. That was over 2000 years ago.

24333.q: Which Roman general stood in the way of the Helvetii in 58 BC?
24333.e: Julius Caesar was governor in Gaul at the time. He did not want the Helvetii to march through Roman territory.

24334.q: According to Caesar, what did the Helvetii do with their villages before they left?
24334.e: According to Caesar, the Helvetii set fire to their houses. That way they could not simply turn back.
24334.m: The Helvetii burnt down their villages before leaving.

24335.q: Where did the Helvetii want to go when they left?
24335.e: The Helvetii wanted to go to the west of Gaul, in present-day France. The Santones tribe lived there.
24335.m: The Helvetii wanted to move west.

24336.q: Near which place were the Helvetii defeated in 58 BC?
24336.e: At Bibracte in Gaul the Helvetii lost a great battle. Bibracte is in present-day France.
24336.m: The Helvetii were defeated at Bibracte.

24337.q: What did the Helvetii have to do after their defeat?
24337.e: The victor sent the Helvetii back to their old territory. There they were to rebuild their villages.
24337.m: After their defeat the Helvetii went home.

24338.q: According to Caesar, how many villages did the Helvetii burn when they left?
24338.e: Caesar writes of about 400 villages and twelve fortified towns. But researchers have found only a few traces of fire.
24338.m: According to Caesar, about 400 villages were burnt.

24339.q: What did the Helvetii take with them when they left?
24339.e: According to Caesar, whole families set off with carts and animals. Today, however, researchers doubt his high numbers.
24339.m: Whole families went along when the Helvetii left.

24340.e: Divico was a famous Celtic leader. He lived over 2000 years ago.
24340.m: Divico was a leader of the Helvetii.

24341.q: Against whom did Divico win a battle in 107 BC?
24341.e: Divico defeated a Roman army under the general Lucius Cassius Longinus. That was a great success for his people.

24342.q: Against whom did the Helvetian leader Divico win a famous battle?
24342.e: In 107 BC Divico defeated a Roman army in what is now France.

24343.q: Roughly how old was Divico in 58 BC?
24343.e: Divico was born around 130 BC. So in 58 BC he was already an old man.
24343.m: In 58 BC Divico was already an old man.

24344.q: What did Caesar demand in the negotiations with Divico?
24344.e: Hostages are people who have to be handed over as a guarantee. This way Caesar wanted to be sure that the Helvetii would obey.
24344.m: Caesar demanded hostages from the Helvetii.

24345.q: Caesar demanded hostages from the Helvetii. How did their leader Divico reply?
24345.e: Divico said the Helvetii were used to taking hostages, not giving them. The negotiations failed.

24346.q: What did the defeated Romans have to do after Divico’s victory?
a: Make sacrifices to the gods of the Helvetii
24346.e: A yoke was a frame made of spears. Anyone who had to walk under it was humiliated in front of everyone.
24346.m: The Romans had to walk under the yoke.

24347.q: What was Divico like when he met Caesar almost 50 years after his victory?
24347.e: Caesar writes that Divico was already very old at that time. He had won his victory over the Romans about 50 years earlier.
24347.m: Divico was already very old when he met Caesar.

24348.q: In which canton is the Roman theatre of Augusta Raurica?
24348.e: The Roman town of Augusta Raurica lies in the canton of Basel-Landschaft and reaches into Aargau. The theatre is one of the best-known Roman buildings in Switzerland.
24348.m: The theatre of Augusta Raurica is in Basel-Landschaft.

24349.q: Roughly how many spectators fitted into the theatre of Augusta Raurica?
24349.e: In its last building phase the theatre held about 10,000 to 12,000 people. That was a huge crowd for the time.
24349.m: About 10,000 people fitted into the theatre of Augusta Raurica.

24350.q: What kind of great treasure was found in Kaiseraugst near Augusta Raurica?
24350.e: The Kaiseraugst silver treasure consists of 270 pieces such as plates, spoons and coins. It weighs about 58 kilograms.
24350.m: A great silver treasure was found in Kaiseraugst.

24352.q: Which river is Augusta Raurica on?
24352.e: The Roman town lay on the south bank of the Rhine. Goods could be transported on the river.
24352.m: Augusta Raurica is on the Rhine.

24353.q: What shape is a Roman theatre like the one in Augusta Raurica?
24353.e: The rows of seats in a Roman theatre are arranged in a semicircle. That way everyone can see the stage well.
24353.m: A Roman theatre is built in a semicircle.

24354.q: Which festival takes place every summer in Augusta Raurica?
24354.e: At the Roman Festival in August, people in costume show how the Romans lived. It is the biggest festival of its kind in Switzerland.
24354.m: Every year Augusta Raurica celebrates the Roman Festival.

24355.q: In which year was Augusta Raurica founded?
24355.e: An inscription on a tomb gives its founding as 44 BC. But the town was only properly built up about 30 years later.
24355.m: Augusta Raurica was founded in 44 BC.

24357.q: In which present-day municipality was Vindonissa?
24357.e: The camp was in Windisch. The present-day name developed from the Latin name.

24358.q: In which canton is the old legionary camp of Vindonissa?
24358.e: Vindonissa is in the canton of Aargau. Important routes and rivers meet there.

24359.q: Between which two rivers was Vindonissa?
24359.e: The camp stood where the Reuss flows into the Aare. The Limmat also joins very close by.
24359.m: Vindonissa lay between the Aare and the Reuss.

24360.q: How many Roman legionary camps were there in what is now Switzerland?
24360.e: Vindonissa was the only legionary camp in what is now Switzerland. Other camps were smaller.
24360.m: There was only one legionary camp in Switzerland.

24361.q: What from Vindonissa is still working today?
24361.e: A Roman water pipe still brings water to a fountain today. It is almost 2000 years old.
24361.m: A Roman water pipe still flows today.

24362.q: What is the attraction near the old camp of Vindonissa called where you can discover soldiers’ life?
24362.e: On the Legionary Trail you can put on Roman clothes. You can even spend the night in rebuilt barracks.
24362.m: On the Legionary Trail you experience the life of soldiers.

24363.q: What was Vindonissa, near present-day Windisch?
a: A Roman port by the sea
24363.e: Thousands of Roman soldiers lived in Vindonissa in the canton of Aargau. It was the only legionary camp in what is now Switzerland. The legion left in AD 101.
24363.m: Vindonissa was a Roman legionary camp in Switzerland.

24364.q: In which town is the Vindonissa Museum?
24364.e: The Vindonissa Museum is in Brugg, right next to Windisch. You can see many finds from the camp there.
24364.m: The Vindonissa Museum is in Brugg.

24365.q: What is the town of Aventicum called today?
24365.e: Aventicum is near the present-day small town of Avenches. Many Roman ruins can still be seen there.

24366.e: Avenches belongs to the canton of Vaud in western Switzerland. French is spoken there.
24366.m: Aventicum is in the canton of Vaud.

24367.q: Which Roman building can still be seen in Avenches today?
24367.e: The Roman amphitheatre still stands in Avenches. The tower above its entrance now houses the Roman Museum.
24367.m: There is a Roman amphitheatre in Avenches.

24368.q: How many people lived in Aventicum at its height?
24368.e: At its height more than 20,000 people lived in Aventicum. That is many more than in present-day Avenches.
24368.m: Over 20,000 people once lived in Aventicum.

24369.q: What protected the Roman town of Aventicum against attackers?
a: A long town wall with towers
24369.e: A wall over 5 kilometres long with many towers ran around Aventicum. One tower, the Tornallaz, has been rebuilt.
24369.m: Aventicum had a long town wall with towers.

24370.q: What did people watch in the amphitheatre of Aventicum?
24370.e: In the amphitheatre gladiators fought and there were animal hunts. Chariot races, on the other hand, took place in a circus.

24371.q: The tall column in Aventicum is called the “Cigognier”. Which bird once nested on it?
24371.e: “Cigogne” is the French word for stork. For a long time a stork had its nest on the 12-metre-high column.
24371.m: The Cigognier column is named after the stork.

24372.q: Which lake is Aventicum very close to?
24372.e: Aventicum had a harbour on Lake Murten. Over lakes and rivers, ships could travel as far as the Rhine.
24372.m: Aventicum is close to Lake Murten.

24373.q: Which Roman emperor does the famous golden bust from Avenches show?
24373.e: The bust shows Emperor Marcus Aurelius with a beard and curly hair. He was a Roman emperor.
24373.m: The golden bust from Avenches shows Marcus Aurelius.

24374.q: What metal is the emperor’s bust from Avenches mainly made of?
24374.e: The bust is about 92 per cent gold. That is very rare for a Roman bust.
24374.m: The emperor’s bust from Avenches is made of gold.

24375.q: In which year was the golden emperor’s bust found in Avenches?
24375.e: Workers found the bust on 19 April 1939. It was a huge surprise.
24375.m: The golden bust was found in 1939.

24376.q: Where exactly was the golden emperor’s bust when it was found?
24376.e: The bust lay in a Roman drain under a temple. Perhaps it was hidden there from robbers.
24376.m: The bust lay in a Roman drain.

24377.q: Roughly how heavy is the golden bust of Marcus Aurelius?
24377.e: The bust weighs 1.589 kilograms. The gold is hammered as thin as sheet metal.
24377.m: The gold bust weighs about 1.6 kilograms.

a: A sculpture of the head and shoulders
A whole statue of a rider
24378.e: A bust shows only a person’s head, neck and shoulders. You do not see the rest of the body.
24378.m: A bust shows the head and shoulders.

24379.q: Where is the original golden bust of Marcus Aurelius kept today?
a: In the Federal Palace in Bern
24379.e: For safety, the original is kept in the vault of a bank in Vaud. There is a copy in the Roman Museum in Avenches.
24379.m: The original gold bust is in a bank vault.

24380.q: In which century did Emperor Marcus Aurelius rule?
24380.e: Marcus Aurelius ruled from AD 161 to 180. That is the 2nd century.
24380.m: Marcus Aurelius ruled in the 2nd century AD.

24381.e: On an estate, fields were farmed and animals were kept. It included a house and many outbuildings.
24381.m: A Roman estate was a large farm.

24382.q: What is a Roman farming estate called in Latin?
24382.e: “Villa rustica” means “country house”. There were many such estates in Switzerland.
24382.m: A farming estate is called a villa rustica in Latin.

24383.q: How were rich Roman country houses heated in winter?
a: With warm air under the floor
With hot stones in the bed
24383.e: Hot air from the fire flowed under the floor and through the walls. This heating is called a hypocaust.
24383.m: The Romans already had underfloor heating.

24384.q: Which Roman estate in the canton of Zurich is well known?
24384.e: The Seeb estate is near Winkel in the Zurich Unterland. You can visit the walls and a small museum.
24384.m: A Roman estate stood at Seeb.

24385.q: What is the Roman estate of Orbe-Boscéaz famous for?
24385.e: At Orbe in the canton of Vaud you can see splendid floor pictures. They show gods and animals, for example.
24385.m: There are beautiful Roman mosaics at Orbe.

24386.q: What is a Roman mosaic made of?
24386.e: A mosaic is put together from lots of tiny coloured stones. This makes a picture on the floor.
24386.m: A mosaic is made of tiny stones.

24387.q: Where did the owner of a Roman estate live?
24387.e: The owner lived in the fine main house with a bath and heating. Workers and animals lived in other buildings.
24387.m: The owner lived in the main house.

24388.q: Which plant did the Romans spread in Switzerland for a drink?
24388.e: The Romans liked drinking wine and planted vines. Coffee, tea and cocoa only came to Europe much later.

24389.q: In which canton is the Julier Pass, which the Romans already used?
24389.e: The Julier Pass is in the Grisons and is 2284 metres high. It links the Oberhalbstein with the Engadine.
24389.m: The Julier Pass is in the Grisons.

24390.q: What can still be seen at the top of the Julier Pass today?
24390.e: Remains of columns stand next to the pass road. They belonged to a Roman shrine.
24390.m: Remains of Roman columns stand on the Julier Pass.

24391.q: Which areas does the Great St Bernard Pass link?
24391.e: The pass leads from Valais into the Aosta Valley in Italy. For the Romans it was an important route to Gaul.
24391.m: The Great St Bernard links Valais with Italy.

24392.q: Which god was a temple on the Great St Bernard dedicated to?
24392.e: The Celts worshipped the god Poeninus there. The Romans equated him with Jupiter.
24392.m: A temple to Jupiter stood on the Great St Bernard.

24393.q: Roughly how high is the Great St Bernard Pass?
24393.e: The pass is 2469 metres above sea level. In winter it is closed for a long time because of snow.
24393.m: The Great St Bernard is almost 2500 metres high.

24394.q: What did the milestones on Roman roads show?
24394.e: Milestones were stone columns at the side of the road. They said how far it was to a certain town.

24395.q: How did people travel on Roman roads?
a: On foot, on horseback or by cart
24395.e: The Romans walked, rode or travelled by cart. They did not need elephants and camels for this.
24395.m: On Roman roads people travelled on foot, on horseback or by cart.

24396.q: Why did the Romans build good roads over the Alps?
a: So that soldiers and traders could travel fast
So that herders could take their herds up to the alpine pastures
So that mountain farmers could bring wood down to the valley
So that gladiators could get to Rome
24396.e: On good roads soldiers and goods moved faster. That way the Romans could hold their great empire together.
24396.m: The Romans built roads for soldiers and trade.

24397.e: The name Zurich developed from the old name Turicum. Turicum was a small Roman settlement.

24398.q: What was there in the Roman settlement of Turicum?
24398.e: In Turicum traders had to pay customs duty on their goods. A border between two Roman provinces ran here.
24398.m: People paid customs duty in Turicum.

24399.q: On which hill in Zurich did a Roman fort stand?
24399.e: On the Lindenhof the Romans built a fortress with ten towers. Today there is a square with trees there.
24399.m: A Roman fort stood on the Lindenhof.

24400.q: Where was the name Turicum found for the first time?
24400.e: In 1747 a gravestone for a small child was found. The child’s father was the head of the customs post.
24400.m: A gravestone is the first to mention the name Turicum.

24401.e: Turicum lay where the Limmat flows out of Lake Zurich. Goods could easily be reloaded there.

24402.q: What from Roman times was found near the Weinplatz in Zurich?
24402.e: In the Thermengasse near the Weinplatz, remains of Roman baths were discovered in 1983. The lane is named after these baths.
24402.m: A Roman bath stood near the Weinplatz in Zurich.

24404.q: Who was the Roman fort in Zurich meant to protect against?
24404.e: In the 4th century the Alemanni attacked the Roman Empire. That is why the Romans built strong walls around their towns.
24404.m: The fort in Zurich protected against the Alemanni.

24405.q: Which town was called Lousonna in Roman times?
24405.e: Lousonna was a Roman settlement on the lakeshore. Lausanne later developed from it.

24406.e: Lousonna lay right on the shore of Lake Geneva. It had a harbour there.

24407.q: Which present-day Swiss city was called Lousonna in Roman times?
24407.e: The Roman settlement of Lousonna lay on Lake Geneva in what is now the Vidy district of Lausanne. There is a Roman museum there.

24408.q: Which well-known organisation has its headquarters today where Lousonna once was?
24408.e: The headquarters of the Olympic Committee stands in Vidy. Remains of the Roman settlement lie underneath and beside it.
24408.m: The Olympic Committee is now based where Lousonna lay.

24409.q: How did the Romans in Lousonna move heavy goods across Lake Geneva?
a: With pack animals along the shore
24409.e: An inscription by boatmen shows that there was shipping on the lake. Heavy goods travelled well on the water.
24409.m: The Romans transported goods across the lake by ship.

24410.q: Which people lived in Genava when the Romans came?
24410.e: At that time Celtic tribes lived in the area around Genava. The Romans called the region Gaul.

24411.q: Which river flows out of the lake in Geneva?
24411.e: In Geneva the Rhône leaves the lake. It then flows on into France.
24411.m: In Geneva the Rhône flows out of the lake.

24412.q: What did Caesar have destroyed in Genava in 58 BC to stop the Helvetii?
24412.e: Without a bridge the Helvetii could not easily cross the river. That way Caesar blocked their path.
24412.m: Caesar had the bridge in Genava destroyed.

24413.q: In which famous book is Genava first mentioned?
24413.e: Julius Caesar described his wars in Gaul in a book. In it he also mentions Genava.
24413.m: Genava appears in Caesar’s book about the Gallic War.

24414.q: Which present-day town did the Romans call Vitudurum?
24414.e: Vitudurum was a Roman settlement in the district of Oberwinterthur. It later became Winterthur.

24415.q: Which present-day town did the Romans call Salodurum?
24415.e: Salodurum lay on the Aare. Over time the name became Solothurn.

24416.q: Which present-day town did the Romans call Curia?
24416.e: Curia was a Roman town in Raetia. Today Chur is the capital of the Grisons.

24417.q: Which present-day city did the Romans call Basilia?
24417.e: Basilia lay on the Rhine on the Minster hill. The name Basel came from it.

24418.q: Which people do many place names ending in “-dunum” and “-durum”, such as Eburodunum or Salodurum, come from?
24418.e: The Celts lived in the area of Switzerland before the Romans. The Romans took over many Celtic place names, for example Salodurum for Solothurn.
24418.m: Place names ending in -dunum and -durum are Celtic.

24419.q: Which present-day town did the Romans call Aquae Helveticae?
24419.e: “Aquae” means “waters”. Baden has warm springs where even the Romans bathed.

24420.q: Which present-day town on Lake Constance did the Romans call Arbor Felix?
24420.e: Arbor Felix means “happy tree”. The name later became Arbon.

24421.q: Which present-day town on Lake Geneva did the Romans call Noviodunum?
24421.e: Noviodunum was a Celtic name. The Romans founded a colony there, which became Nyon.

24422.q: Which present-day town did the Romans call Eburodunum?
24422.e: Eburodunum lay at the southern end of Lake Neuchâtel. Today the town is called Yverdon-les-Bains.

24423.q: Which present-day place is where the Roman town of Augusta Raurica was?
24423.e: Augusta Raurica was a large Roman town on the Rhine near Basel. Today the villages of Augst and Kaiseraugst are there.
24423.m: Augusta Raurica was at present-day Augst.

24424.q: What do you call a boy who begins his training as a knight in a castle at about 7 years old?
24424.e: Training to be a knight usually began at about 7, as a page. The page lived at a lord’s court and served him.
24424.m: At about 7, a boy became a page.

24425.q: What is a young man called who serves a knight and wants to become a knight himself?
24425.e: The squire helped a knight and learned fighting from him. Later he could become a knight himself.
24425.m: A squire serves a knight and learns from him.

24426.q: At about what age did a page become a squire?
24426.e: At about 14, a page was solemnly made a squire. Then his training with weapons began.
24426.m: At about 14, a page became a squire.

24427.q: What did a page learn first at court?
24427.e: A page served at table and learned how to behave properly at court. He also had his first riding lessons.
24427.m: A page first learned good manners at court.

24428.q: What did a squire help his knight with before a fight?
24428.e: It was almost impossible to put on armour by yourself. The squire helped the knight with it and also looked after his weapons.
24428.m: The squire helped the knight into his armour.

24429.q: Which of the knight’s animals did a squire have to look after?
24429.e: The squire made sure his knight’s horse was cared for. In battle he often also led a spare horse.
24429.m: A squire looked after his knight’s horse.

24430.q: What did a squire hand his knight at a tournament when his lance had broken?
24430.e: At tournaments and in battle, the squire brought the knight new weapons. Lances in particular often broke.
24430.m: The squire brought his knight new weapons.

24433.q: With what did the lord touch the squire’s shoulder when knighting him?
24433.e: The lord laid the flat side of his sword on the squire’s shoulder. That was the sign of knighting.
24433.m: When someone is knighted, a sword touches their shoulder.

24434.q: At about what age was a squire knighted?
24434.e: A squire could become a knight at about 21. Before that he had to prove his courage and loyalty.
24434.m: At about 21, a squire could become a knight.

24435.q: What did the squire do in front of his lord when he was knighted?
24435.e: The squire knelt down in front of his lord. That was how he showed his respect.
24435.m: When being knighted, the squire kneels down.

24436.q: What did a new knight promise his lord?
24436.e: The new knight swore to serve his lord loyally. Loyalty was very important for knights.
24436.m: A knight promised his lord loyalty.

24437.e: Only someone who was a knight himself, or a great lord such as a king, was allowed to knight someone.
24437.m: Only a knight or a ruler could knight someone.

24438.q: Who still knights people in Great Britain today?
24438.e: In Great Britain the King, as of 2026 King Charles III, knights people who deserve it. Today it is an honour for special achievements.
24438.m: Knighthoods still exist in Great Britain today.

24439.q: Which title does a man in Great Britain receive when he is knighted?
24439.e: A man who is knighted in Great Britain is called “Sir” afterwards. One example is the musician Sir Paul McCartney.
24439.m: A British knight is addressed as Sir.

24440.q: What is a coat of arms?
24440.e: A coat of arms is a coloured emblem. It belongs to a family, a town or a country.
24440.m: A coat of arms is a coloured sign of recognition.

24441.q: Why did knights paint a coat of arms on their shield?
a: So that people could recognise them
So that the shield brought luck
24441.e: In armour and with a helmet, one knight looked just like another. You could recognise him by the coat of arms on his shield.
24441.m: You recognised a knight in armour by his coat of arms.

24442.q: What does the Swiss coat of arms show?
24442.e: The Swiss coat of arms shows a white cross on a red background. You see the same emblem on the Swiss flag.
24442.m: The Swiss coat of arms has a white cross on red.

24443.q: Which animal is on the coat of arms of Bern?
24443.e: A black bear walks across the coat of arms of Bern. The bear is the heraldic animal of the city and canton of Bern.
24443.m: The bear is the heraldic animal of Bern.

24444.q: What does the coat of arms of the canton of Uri show?
24444.e: The coat of arms of Uri shows a black bull’s head on a yellow background. It is called the Uri bull.
24444.m: There is a bull’s head on the coat of arms of Uri.

24445.q: Which animal appears most often on coats of arms?
24445.e: The lion is the most common heraldic animal. It stands for courage and strength.
24445.m: The lion is the most common animal on coats of arms.

24446.q: What does the coat of arms of the canton of Basel-Stadt show?
24446.e: The coat of arms of Basel-Stadt shows a black Basel crozier on white. The staff is a reminder of the Bishop of Basel.
24446.m: Basel-Stadt has a black Basel crozier on its coat of arms.

24447.q: What shape is a coat of arms usually?
24447.e: Coats of arms began on the shields of knights. That is why they still usually have the shape of a shield today.
24447.m: A coat of arms usually has the shape of a shield.

24449.q: At a tournament, what did two knights use to try to knock each other off their horses?
24449.e: Two knights rode towards each other. With their long lances they tried to hit their opponent or lift him out of the saddle.
24449.m: At tournaments, knights fought with lances.

24450.q: Why did tournament lances often have a blunt tip?
a: So that nobody got badly hurt
So that they could be thrown
24450.e: Nobody was supposed to be killed at a tournament. That is why the lances were often blunt, but there were still injuries.
24450.m: Tournament lances were blunt so that nobody got badly hurt.

24451.q: In later jousting, what separated the two riders?
24451.e: Later a wooden barrier was put up between the riders. That way the horses could not crash into each other.
24451.m: A wooden barrier separated the riders when jousting.

24452.q: What did a defeated knight often have to give the winner at a tournament?
24452.e: A defeated knight often had to hand over his horse and armour to the winner. He could also buy them back with money.
24452.m: Whoever lost a tournament often had to give up his horse and armour.

24453.q: What else were tournaments useful for to knights?
24453.e: At tournaments, knights practised fighting on horseback. That way they were prepared for war.
24453.m: At tournaments, knights practised for war.

24454.q: What did a knight sometimes receive from a lady before competing in a tournament?
24454.e: A lady sometimes gave a knight a cloth or a sleeve. The knight wore it at the tournament as a sign of her favour.
24454.m: At tournaments, a knight sometimes wore his lady’s cloth.

24455.q: What do you call a tournament fight in which many knights fight each other in groups?
24455.e: In a melee, two groups of riders charged at each other. They usually fought with blunt weapons.
24455.m: In a melee, groups of knights fought against each other.

24456.q: What is chain mail made of?
24456.e: Chain mail is made of thousands of small iron rings. Each ring is linked to several others.
24456.m: Chain mail is made of lots of small iron rings.

24457.q: What did a knight wear under his chain mail?
24457.e: Under the chain mail, people wore a thickly padded shirt. It softened blows and protected the skin from the rings.
24457.m: A padded shirt was worn under chain mail.

24458.q: What did chain mail protect especially well against?
24458.e: The iron rings kept out the edge of a sword well. Against hard blows, it was mainly the padding underneath that helped.

24459.q: Roughly how heavy was a shirt of chain mail?
24459.e: A simple shirt of chain mail with short sleeves weighed about 15 kilograms. The weight was spread over the whole body.
24459.m: A shirt of chain mail weighed about 15 kilograms.

24460.q: What is the later armour made of large metal plates called?
24460.e: In the late Middle Ages, knights wore armour made of large steel plates. It is called plate armour.
24460.m: Later, knights wore plate armour made of metal.

24461.q: What protected a knight’s head in battle?
24461.e: Knights wore a metal helmet. It protected the head from sword blows.
24461.m: The helmet protected the knight’s head.

24462.q: Why did a great helm have narrow slits at the front?
a: To tie it to the saddle
24462.e: Through the narrow eye slits the knight could look out. Small holes helped with breathing.
24462.m: The knight could see through the slits in his helmet.

24463.q: What is the part of a helmet that you can flip up in front of your face called?
24463.e: The visor protects the face. You can flip it up to see and breathe better.
24463.m: The visor is the hinged face guard on a helmet.

24464.q: On an early knight’s helmet, what protected the nose?
24464.e: Early helmets had a strip of metal at the front over the nose. It is called a nasal.
24464.m: A strip of metal on the helmet protected the nose.

24465.q: What do you call the strong horse a knight rode into battle?
24465.e: The warhorse was a strong, well-trained fighting horse. It had to be able to carry a knight in armour.
24465.m: A knight rode into battle on a warhorse.

24466.q: How expensive was a good warhorse?
a: As expensive as a loaf of bread
24466.e: A good warhorse cost a lot of money. Only rich people could afford such a horse.

24467.q: Were warhorses mostly stallions or mares?
24467.e: Stallions were usually chosen as warhorses. They were seen as strong and brave.

24468.q: What did a knight use at his heels to urge his horse on?
24468.e: Spurs are small metal parts on the boots. With them, the knight gave signals to the horse.
24468.m: A knight urged his horse on with spurs.

24469.q: What helped a knight stay firmly on his horse when striking with his lance?
24469.e: The knight could brace his feet firmly in the stirrups. That made him less likely to fall off when striking with the lance.
24469.m: The stirrups gave the knight a firm hold.

24470.q: What did a warhorse have to learn in training?
a: To stay calm in the noise of battle
24470.e: A warhorse must not run away in noise and chaos. That is why it was trained for a long time.
24470.m: A warhorse learned to stay calm in the noise.

24471.q: What did a warhorse sometimes wear for protection?
24471.e: Some warhorses wore armour made of metal or leather. It mainly protected the head and chest.

24472.q: What did a horse often wear that showed the knight’s coat of arms?
24472.e: A colourful cloth with the coat of arms was often laid over the horse. That way you could recognise the knight from far away.
24472.m: The horse’s covering often showed the knight’s coat of arms.

24473.q: Why did a knight often ride a different horse from his warhorse when travelling?
a: Because the warhorse was too small
24473.e: The valuable warhorse was meant to be rested for battle. So on journeys, the knight rode another horse.
24473.m: The warhorse was spared for battle.

24474.e: A virtue is a good quality in a person. Knights were supposed to have many virtues.
24474.m: A virtue is a good quality.

24475.q: What did the virtue of “loyalty” mean for a knight?
24475.e: Loyalty meant always staying true to your lord and to your word. A loyal knight did not let his lord down.
24475.m: Loyalty means standing by your lord.

24476.q: Whom was a knight supposed to protect?
24476.e: A good knight was supposed to help the weak, the poor, widows and orphans. That was part of the ideals of knighthood.
24476.m: A knight was supposed to protect the weak.

24477.q: Which word does the word “courteous” come from?
24477.e: At a prince’s court, you had to behave well. That is why “courteous” comes from the word “court”.
24477.m: The word courteous comes from the word court.

24478.q: Which virtue means being brave in danger?
24478.e: Bravery means acting courageously in danger. This virtue was very important for knights.

24479.q: Which virtue means keeping to the right measure and not overdoing things?
24479.e: Moderation means not overdoing it with food, drink or anger. In the Middle Ages this was called “mâze”.
24479.m: Moderation means keeping to the right measure.

24480.q: A good knight was supposed to be generous. What does that mean?
24480.e: A noble knight was supposed to be glad to give things to others. This virtue was called generosity.
24480.m: Being generous means being happy to share.

24481.q: What did a knight lose if he was a coward or broke his word?
24481.e: Honour was very important to a knight. Anyone who was cowardly or lied was no longer respected by the others.
24481.m: A knight did not want to lose his honour.

a: The unmarried daughter of a castle lord
24482.e: A castle maiden is the daughter of a castle lord who is not yet married. She lived with her family in the castle.
24482.m: A castle maiden is an unmarried daughter living in the castle.

24483.q: What did girls in a castle often learn?
24483.e: Girls in the castle learned needlework such as spinning, weaving and embroidery. They also learned good manners.
24483.m: Castle maidens often learned spinning and embroidery.

24484.q: What do you call the wife of a castle lord?
24484.e: The wife of the castle lord is called the lady of the castle. She had a lot of say in the castle.
24484.m: The wife of the castle lord is called the lady of the castle.

24485.q: Who often ran the castle when the lord was away at war?
24485.e: When the lord was away, his wife often ran the castle. She took care of supplies, servants and order.
24485.m: The lady of the castle often ran it when her husband was away.

24486.q: Who usually decided whom a castle maiden should marry?
24486.e: In noble families, marriages were often decided by the parents. It was about land, power and alliances.
24486.m: Usually the family decided whom a castle maiden married.

24487.q: Which board game did nobles like to play in the castle?
24487.e: Chess came to Europe in the Middle Ages and became very popular with the nobility. Noblewomen often played chess too.
24487.m: Chess was popular with nobles in the Middle Ages.

24488.q: Which hat do castle maidens often wear in pictures from the late Middle Ages?
24488.e: In the late Middle Ages, noblewomen sometimes wore a tall pointed hat. A fine veil often hung from it.
24488.m: Noblewomen sometimes wore a tall pointed hat.

24489.q: What could noblewomen in the Middle Ages often do better than many knights?
24489.e: Many noblewomen learned to read, for example from prayer books. Many knights, on the other hand, could not read.

24490.e: A herald delivered his lord’s messages. He also announced important news in public.
24490.m: A herald was a messenger and announcer.

24491.q: Who knew a lot about coats of arms in the Middle Ages?
24491.e: The herald had to know the knights’ coats of arms. That way he knew who was at the tournament or on the battlefield.
24491.m: A herald knew the knights’ coats of arms.

24492.q: What did the herald announce at a tournament?
24492.e: At the tournament, the herald introduced the knights and called out their names. He also made sure the rules were kept.
24492.m: At tournaments, the herald called out the knights’ names.

24493.q: Which word for the study of coats of arms comes from the word “herald”?
24493.e: The study of coats of arms is called heraldry. The name comes from the heralds, who knew all about coats of arms.
24493.m: Heraldry is named after the herald.

24494.q: What was the rule for a herald who brought a message to the enemy?
a: Nobody was allowed to harm him.
He had to be locked up.
24494.e: A herald was considered untouchable. Even the enemy was not allowed to harm him, so that messages arrived safely.
24494.m: Nobody was allowed to harm a herald.

24495.q: What did a herald wear over his clothes?
a: A tunic with his lord’s coat of arms
24495.e: The herald wore a tabard with his lord’s coat of arms. That way everyone could see on whose behalf he came.
24495.m: A herald wore his lord’s coat of arms.

24496.q: What was often used to announce a herald?
24496.e: Before the herald spoke, trumpeters often played. That way everyone listened.

24497.q: Where did a herald often announce the ruler’s orders?
24497.e: Many people gathered in the market square. There the herald called out orders and news.
24497.m: The herald announced news in the market square.

24498.q: What is the round table of King Arthur and his knights called?
24498.e: King Arthur sat with his knights at the Round Table. At a round table, nobody was more important than anyone else.
24498.m: At the Round Table, all knights were equally important.

24499.q: What is the name of King Arthur’s famous sword?
24499.e: Excalibur is King Arthur’s magic sword. In some stories he received it from the Lady of the Lake.
24499.m: King Arthur’s sword is called Excalibur.

24500.q: In the legend, what did the young Arthur pull a sword out of?
24500.e: Only the true king could pull the sword from the stone. The young Arthur managed it.
24500.m: Arthur pulled the sword from the stone.

24501.q: What is the name of the wizard who helps King Arthur?
24501.e: Merlin is the wise wizard in the Arthurian legends. He advised King Arthur.

24502.q: What is the name of King Arthur’s castle?
24502.e: Camelot is King Arthur’s castle and court. The Round Table stood there too.
24502.m: King Arthur’s castle is called Camelot.

24503.q: What is the name of King Arthur’s wife?
24503.e: Guinevere is the queen and Arthur’s wife. In German she is also called Ginover.

24504.q: Which knight of the Round Table fell in love with the queen?
24504.e: Lancelot was one of Arthur’s best knights. He fell in love with Queen Guinevere.

24505.q: In many stories, what were the knights of the Round Table searching for?
24505.e: The Holy Grail is a mysterious vessel. Many knights of the Round Table set out to search for it.
24505.m: Arthur’s knights searched for the Holy Grail.

24506.q: Which country do the legends of King Arthur come from?
24506.e: The Arthurian legends come from Britain. Later they were told all over Europe.
24506.m: The legends of King Arthur come from Britain.

24507.q: In which forest did Robin Hood live?
24507.e: Robin Hood lived with his friends in Sherwood Forest. This forest is near the town of Nottingham.
24507.m: Robin Hood lived in Sherwood Forest.

24508.q: In the stories, whom did Robin Hood take money from to give to the poor?
24508.e: Robin Hood took money from the rich and gave it to the poor. That is why he is a hero in many stories.
24508.m: Robin Hood took from the rich and gave to the poor.

24509.q: Which weapon was Robin Hood especially good with?
24509.e: Robin Hood was a very good archer. His arrows almost always hit the target.
24509.m: Robin Hood was a master with bow and arrow.

24510.q: Who is Robin Hood’s great enemy?
24510.e: The Sheriff of Nottingham wants to catch Robin Hood. In the stories he is his greatest enemy.
24510.m: The Sheriff of Nottingham hunts Robin Hood.

24511.q: What is the name of Robin Hood’s sweetheart?
24511.e: Maid Marian is Robin Hood’s sweetheart. In some stories she is called Lady Marian.

24513.q: Which of Robin Hood’s friends is a fat, cheerful monk?
24513.e: Friar Tuck is a monk who lives in the forest with Robin Hood. He loves eating and laughing.
24513.m: Friar Tuck is the monk with Robin Hood.

24514.q: What colour are Robin Hood’s clothes usually?
24514.e: Robin Hood usually wears green clothes. That way he is well hidden in the forest.

24515.q: In which country are the stories of Robin Hood set?
24515.e: The stories of Robin Hood are set in England. The town of Nottingham is there.
24515.m: Robin Hood is a hero from England.

a: A poet and singer of love songs
A guard at the castle gate
24516.e: A minnesinger wrote songs and performed them himself. He was both poet and singer.

24517.q: What does the old German word “Minne” mean?
24517.e: “Minne” is an old German word for love. So Minnesang means love song.
24517.m: Minne is an old word for love.

24518.q: Whom did a minnesinger usually sing his songs for?
24518.e: In his songs, the minnesinger praised a noble lady. Often she was out of his reach.
24518.m: Minnesingers sang for a noble lady.

24519.q: Who is probably the most famous minnesinger?
24519.e: This poet lived around 1200. He is considered the most famous minnesinger.
24519.m: Walther von der Vogelweide was a famous minnesinger.

24520.q: In which Swiss city was the famous song manuscript “Codex Manesse” created?
24520.e: The Codex Manesse was written in Zurich around 1300. It contains songs and colourful pictures of many minnesingers.
24520.m: The Codex Manesse was created in Zurich.

24521.q: What does the Codex Manesse contain?
24521.e: The Codex Manesse is a large manuscript of songs. It contains songs and colourful pictures of many minnesingers.
24521.m: The Codex Manesse contains songs by minnesingers.

24522.q: In which period did the minnesingers live?
a: In the time of the lake dwellers
24522.e: The minnesingers lived in the Middle Ages, especially around the year 1200. They sang at the courts of the nobility.
24522.m: Minnesingers lived in the Middle Ages.

24523.q: Where did minnesingers perform their songs?
a: At the courts of the nobility
24523.e: Minnesingers travelled from court to court. There they sang for the nobles and their guests.
24523.m: Minnesingers sang at the courts of the nobility.

24524.q: In many castles, where did the keep stand?
a: On the side where enemies attacked
In the middle of the moat
24524.e: Many keeps stood on the side from which an attack was most likely to come. That way the strong tower protected the castle like a shield.
24524.m: The keep often stood on the most exposed side of the castle.

24525.q: What could the keep be used for if enemies got into the castle?
24525.e: If the enemies were already in the castle courtyard, the people living there could flee into the keep. How often this really happened is disputed among researchers.
24525.m: The keep was the last refuge of the castle’s inhabitants.

24526.q: Where was the entrance of many keeps?
24526.e: The entrance was often several metres up in the wall. That made it hard for enemies to get in.
24526.m: Many keeps had an entrance high up in the wall.

24527.q: How did people often get up to the high entrance of the keep?
a: Through a tunnel in the ground
24527.e: People climbed up a ladder or a wooden staircase. When there was danger, they simply pulled it in.
24527.m: The ladder to the keep could be pulled in when there was danger.

24528.q: What could a guard at the top of the castle’s tallest tower do well?
24528.e: From the tall tower, the guard could see a long way. That way he spotted enemies early.
24528.m: From the tall castle tower you could see enemies from far away.

24529.q: What do you call a dark prison right at the bottom of a castle tower?
24529.e: A dungeon is a dark prison room without a door. But the room at the very bottom of the tower was often just used for storage.
24529.m: A dungeon is a dark prison in the castle.

24530.q: What do you call a watchman who kept a lookout at the top of a tower?
24530.e: The tower watchman kept watch at the top of the tower. If he saw enemies or fire, he raised the alarm.
24530.m: The tower watchman kept watch at the top of the tower.

24531.q: Why did a keep have very thick walls?
a: So that it could withstand attacks
So that it stayed warm inside
So that it could be built taller
So that supplies could be stored in the walls
24531.e: Thick walls held out against stones and battering rams for a long time. Some walls were several metres thick.
24531.m: Thick walls protected the keep from attacks.

24532.q: What did attackers often try to do with the moat?
a: Fill it with earth and wood
24532.e: A filled-in moat was no longer an obstacle. Then the attackers could get right up to the wall.
24532.m: Attackers filled in the moat to reach the wall.

24533.q: What is the ditch called that separates a castle on a ridge from the rest of the mountain?
24533.e: The neck ditch separated the castle from the rest of the mountain. That way enemies could not simply walk along the ridge to the castle.
24533.m: The neck ditch separates the castle from the mountain.

24534.q: Why was a ditch built around the castle?
a: It made it hard for enemies to reach the wall
There needed to be room for fish
The children could swim in it
Ships were meant to moor there
24534.e: The ditch was an obstacle. Attackers with ladders and battering rams could not get straight to the wall.
24534.m: The ditch keeps attackers away from the castle wall.

24535.q: What do you call a castle moat without water?
24535.e: Many castles on mountains had a ditch without water. It is called a dry moat.
24535.m: A moat without water is called a dry moat.

24536.q: Which part of the castle did the drawbridge lead to?
24536.e: The drawbridge led across the moat straight to the gate. When it was pulled up, it closed the entrance.
24536.m: The drawbridge leads across the moat to the castle gate.

24537.q: What was used to pull up the drawbridge?
24537.e: The bridge hung on chains or ropes. It was pulled up with a winch.
24537.m: The drawbridge was pulled up with chains or ropes.

24538.q: What helped to pull up the heavy drawbridge more easily?
24538.e: Some drawbridges had heavy counterweights. They pulled the bridge up almost by themselves.
24538.m: Counterweights make pulling it up easier.

24539.q: What was a drawbridge usually made of?
24539.e: Wood was light enough for the bridge to be pulled up. It was often strengthened with iron.
24539.m: The drawbridge was usually made of wood.

24540.q: What could be quickly lowered from above in the castle gateway to block it?
24540.e: The portcullis came crashing down in the gateway. That way the entrance was quickly blocked.
24540.m: The portcullis quickly blocks the castle gate.

24541.e: The portcullis blocked the passage through the gate. It protected the way into the castle.
24541.m: The portcullis is in the castle gateway.

24542.q: What was a portcullis made of?
24542.e: Portcullises were made of oak with iron fittings, or entirely of iron. They were very heavy.
24542.m: A portcullis was made of wood and iron.

24543.q: Which animals often pulled the carts with heavy stones to the building site?
24543.e: Oxen are very strong and have great stamina. In the Middle Ages they pulled heavy wagons with stones and wood.
24543.m: Oxen pulled heavy loads to the building site.

24544.q: What did the portcullis often have at the bottom?
24544.e: The bars ended in spikes at the bottom. That way the grille dug into the ground.
24544.m: The portcullis had pointed ends at the bottom.

24545.q: Why did the portcullis close so quickly?
a: It fell down under its own weight
Servants pushed it shut from the side
A water wheel turned it shut
Oxen pulled it shut with ropes
24545.e: You only had to let go of the grille. Because of its great weight, it fell down by itself.
24545.m: The heavy portcullis falls under its own weight.

24546.q: Where was the portcullis when the gate was open?
a: In the room above the gate
24546.e: The grille was pulled up into a room above the gate. From there it could be lowered quickly.
24546.m: The raised portcullis waited above the gate.

24547.q: Some castles had two portcullises in the gateway. What could they do with them?
24547.e: If the guards lowered both grilles, the attackers were trapped in between. They could go neither forwards nor back.
24547.m: Two portcullises could trap enemies in the gateway.

24548.q: What are the gaps between the raised parts of the battlements called?
24548.e: The gaps between the raised parts (merlons) are called crenels or embrasures. The defenders shot through them.
24548.m: The gaps in the battlements are called crenels.

24549.e: A defender could hide behind the raised part of the battlements. He could shoot through the gap next to it.
24549.m: Battlements protected the defenders on the wall.

24550.q: What is a narrow slit in the wall that you could shoot through called?
24550.e: An arrow slit is wide on the inside and narrow on the outside. That way you could shoot out and still be protected.
24550.m: Through an arrow slit you could shoot while staying protected.

24551.q: Which weapon did defenders often shoot from the battlements?
24551.e: Archers stood behind the battlements. Later there were also crossbows.
