a: In large canoes across the sea
25316.e: The ancestors of the Māori came from Polynesia. They sailed across the Pacific in large canoes.
25316.m: The Māori came to New Zealand in canoes.

25317.q: What is New Zealand called in the Māori language?
25317.e: Aotearoa means roughly “land of the long white cloud”.
25317.m: The Māori call New Zealand Aotearoa.

25318.q: What is the famous dance of the Māori called?
25318.e: The haka is a powerful dance with shouting, stamping and pulling faces. New Zealand’s rugby team performs it before matches.
25318.m: The haka is a Māori dance.

25319.q: How do Māori greet each other in the traditional way?
a: They press their noses and foreheads together
25319.e: This greeting is called the hongi. It symbolises sharing the breath of life.
25319.m: Māori greet each other with the hongi.

25320.q: What are the traditional tattoos of the Māori called?
25320.e: Tā moko are artistic lines and spirals, often on the face. They tell of a person’s family and origins.
25320.m: The tattoos of the Māori are called tā moko.

25321.q: Which giant birds did the early Māori hunt until they died out?
25321.e: Moas were flightless running birds without wings, some over three metres tall. They died out a few hundred years ago.
25321.m: The Māori hunted the giant moas.

25322.q: Which country did the seafarer Vasco da Gama come from?
25322.e: Vasco da Gama was a seafarer from Portugal. He sailed on behalf of the Portuguese king.

25323.q: Which country did Vasco da Gama reach by sea in 1498?
25323.e: Vasco da Gama was the first European to find the sea route to India. He landed in the city of Calicut in 1498.
25323.m: Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India.

25324.q: Around which continent did Vasco da Gama sail on his way to India?
25324.e: He sailed south from Portugal along the coast of Africa, around its southern tip and then east.
25324.m: Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa.

25325.q: In which city did Vasco da Gama start his voyage to India in 1497?
25325.e: The voyage began in July 1497 in Lisbon, the capital of Portugal.
25325.m: Vasco da Gama set sail from Lisbon.

25326.q: Which valuable goods did Vasco da Gama mainly bring back from India?
25326.e: In India he bought spices such as pepper. These were worth a great deal in Europe.
25326.m: Vasco da Gama brought precious spices to Portugal.

25327.q: Why was the sea route to India so important for traders?
a: They no longer needed the land route
It had no dangers at all
25327.e: On the long land route, many middlemen took a share of the profit. By ship, traders could fetch the goods directly.
25327.m: By sea, goods could be fetched directly from India.

25328.q: How did Vasco da Gama travel to India?
25328.e: Vasco da Gama crossed the sea with a small fleet of sailing ships.
25328.m: Vasco da Gama travelled by sailing ship.

25329.q: What is Ferdinand Magellan’s voyage famous for?
a: The first voyage around the world
The first voyage around Africa to India
25329.e: Magellan’s fleet was the first to sail all the way around the Earth. This showed that it was possible to sail around the world.
25329.m: Magellan’s fleet was the first to sail around the whole world.

25330.q: For which country did Ferdinand Magellan sail on his great voyage?
25330.e: Magellan came from Portugal. But he made his great voyage on behalf of the Spanish king.

25331.q: What is the name of the sea passage in the south of South America that is named after Magellan?
25331.e: In 1520 Magellan found a passage in the south of South America. This waterway now bears his name.
25331.m: The Strait of Magellan is in the south of South America.

25332.q: What did Ferdinand Magellan’s expedition achieve for the first time?
25332.e: Magellan’s fleet set off in 1519. Magellan himself died on the way, but one of his ships returned in 1522, having sailed once around the Earth.
25332.m: Magellan’s expedition was the first to sail around the whole Earth.

25333.q: What was the name of the only ship that came back from Magellan’s voyage around the world?
25333.e: Only the “Victoria” returned to Spain in 1522. There were still 18 men from the fleet on board.
25333.m: The Victoria was the only ship to complete the voyage around the world.

25334.q: Did Magellan himself live to see the end of his voyage around the world?
a: No, he died on the way
Yes, but he was very ill
No, he stayed in South America
25334.e: Magellan died in 1521 in a battle in the Philippines. Juan Sebastián Elcano led the last ship home.
25334.m: Magellan died during the voyage in the Philippines.

25335.q: Where does the Magellanic penguin live?
a: On the coast of South America
25335.e: The Magellanic penguin lives on the coasts in the south of South America. Magellan’s men saw it there on their voyage.
25335.m: The Magellanic penguin lives in South America.

25336.q: Which seafarer is the continent of America named after?
25336.e: The name America comes from the first name of the seafarer Amerigo Vespucci.
25336.m: America got its name from Amerigo Vespucci.

25337.q: Which city did Amerigo Vespucci come from?
25337.e: Amerigo Vespucci was born in Florence in Italy. At first he worked as a merchant.

25338.q: What did Amerigo Vespucci realise about the newly found land in the west?
25338.e: Many people believed they had landed in Asia. Vespucci wrote that it was a “New World”.
25338.m: Vespucci realised that America is a new continent.

25339.q: What kind of name is “Amerigo” in Amerigo Vespucci?
25339.e: Amerigo is his first name and Vespucci his family name. “Amerigo” became the name America.

25340.q: Where did the name “America” first appear in 1507?
25340.e: In 1507 the mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller wrote the name “America” on his world map.
25340.m: The name America first appeared on a world map.

25341.q: Which part of America did the name “America” refer to on the map of 1507?
25341.e: On Waldseemüller’s map the name was first written on the southern part. That is where Vespucci had sailed.
25341.m: The name America was first written on South America.

25342.e: The caravel was a small wooden sailing ship. The explorers used it to travel far across the sea.
25342.m: The caravel is an explorers’ sailing ship.

25343.q: What material was a caravel built from?
25343.e: Back then, ships were built of wood. Iron and steel came much later.
25343.m: The caravel was built of wood.

25344.q: Which seafarers built the first caravels for their voyages of discovery?
25344.e: The Portuguese used caravels to explore the coast of Africa.
25344.m: The Portuguese went exploring in caravels.

25345.q: What shape were many of a caravel’s sails?
25345.e: Many caravels had triangular sails. This let the ship sail well even when the wind came from the side.

25346.q: What was a big advantage of the caravel?
a: It was fast and easy to steer
25346.e: The caravel was lightly built. That made it fast and easy to steer.
25346.m: The caravel was fast and easy to steer.

25347.e: The caravel had sails. The wind blew into the sails and pushed the ship along.

25348.q: Why could a caravel also sail in shallow water near the coast?
a: It did not sit deep in the water
25348.e: The caravel did not sit deep in the water. That is why it could sail in shallow water too.
25348.m: The caravel could sail in shallow water too.

25349.q: What did seafarers use an astrolabe for?
a: To measure the depth of the water
To measure the strength of the wind
25349.e: With an astrolabe you measured how high the Sun or a star was in the sky. That told you how far north or south you were.
25349.m: The astrolabe helped sailors work out their position.

25350.q: What did people observe with an astrolabe?
25350.e: You pointed the astrolabe at the Sun or a star and then read off its height.
25350.m: The astrolabe was used to observe the Sun and stars.

25351.q: What was a sailor’s astrolabe usually made of?
25351.e: Sailors’ astrolabes were made of brass or bronze. This made them heavy, so they stayed steadier in wind and waves.
25351.m: Sailors’ astrolabes were made of metal.

25352.q: What shape was a sailor’s astrolabe?
25352.e: The astrolabe was a round ring marked with degrees. In the middle, a pointer turned for sighting.

25353.q: What does a nautical chart show?
25353.e: A nautical chart shows coasts, islands, harbours and dangerous places in the sea.
25353.m: A nautical chart shows coasts and seas.

25354.q: Why were old nautical charts often inaccurate?
25354.e: Nobody had seen many of the coasts yet. So they were missing or drawn wrongly.
25354.m: Old charts were inaccurate because so much was unknown.

25355.q: What did explorers add to the maps on their voyages?
25355.e: When explorers saw new land, they drew its coast. In this way the maps kept getting better.
25355.m: Explorers drew new coasts on the maps.

25356.q: What is a compass rose on an old nautical chart?
25356.e: The compass rose is a star with points. It shows north, south, east and west.
25356.m: The compass rose shows the directions.

25357.q: Which country did the pepper come from that the explorers were looking for?
25357.e: Pepper grows in warm countries. A particularly large amount of pepper came from the south of India.

25358.q: What was pepper once called because it was so expensive?
25358.e: Pepper was very precious in Europe. That is why it was called “black gold”.
25358.m: Pepper was as valuable as gold.

25359.e: Peppercorns are the small fruits of the pepper plant, a climbing plant. They are dried, and then they turn black.

25360.q: What were the islands called that were also known as the “Spice Islands”?
25360.e: Cloves and nutmeg grew on the Moluccas in Indonesia. That is why they were called the Spice Islands.
25360.m: The Moluccas are also called the Spice Islands.

25361.q: Which part of the cinnamon tree is cinnamon made from?
25361.e: Cinnamon is the dried bark of the cinnamon tree. As it dries, it rolls up into sticks.

25362.q: On which island did the best cinnamon grow, which the Europeans were looking for?
25362.e: True cinnamon, also called Ceylon cinnamon, comes from Sri Lanka. The island used to be called Ceylon.
25362.m: True cinnamon comes from Sri Lanka.

25363.q: What does a cinnamon stick look like?
25363.e: The bark rolls up as it dries. This is how the brown cinnamon sticks are formed.
25363.m: A cinnamon stick is rolled-up bark.

25364.q: Why was cinnamon so expensive in Europe in the past?
25364.e: Cinnamon had to be brought to Europe along a very long route. That made it rare and expensive.
25364.m: Cinnamon was expensive because it came from far away.

25365.q: Which country did the seafarer James Cook come from?
25365.e: James Cook was a British seafarer from England. He sailed for the British navy.

25366.q: What was the name of James Cook’s ship on his first great voyage?
25366.e: From 1768 to 1771 Cook sailed around the world in the “Endeavour”.
25366.m: Cook’s first ship was called the Endeavour.

25367.q: Which ocean is also called the “South Seas”?
25367.e: The South Seas are the southern Pacific with its many islands. Cook often travelled there.
25367.m: The South Seas are in the Pacific.

25368.q: Which coast of Australia did James Cook explore in 1770?
25368.e: In 1770 Cook sailed along the east coast of Australia and drew it on a map.
25368.m: Cook explored the east coast of Australia.

25369.q: How many great voyages of discovery did James Cook make?
25369.e: Cook made three great voyages to the Pacific. He did not return from the third one.
25369.m: James Cook made three great voyages.

25370.q: On which islands did James Cook die in 1779?
25370.e: On Hawaii there was a quarrel with the inhabitants. Cook was killed in it.

25371.q: Which country made up of two large islands did James Cook sail around and map accurately?
25371.e: Cook sailed all the way around New Zealand. He showed that it consists of two large islands.
25371.m: Cook drew an accurate map of New Zealand.

25372.q: Which unknown land did James Cook search for far in the south on his second voyage?
25372.e: People believed in a great southern land. Cook sailed far south into the ice but found no land where people could live.
25372.m: Cook searched for a great southern land in the south.

25373.q: Which continent does the potato come from?
25373.e: The potato comes from the Andes in South America. The Spanish brought it to Europe.
25373.m: The potato comes from South America.

25374.q: Which well-known Swiss dish is made from potatoes?
25374.e: For rösti, you grate potatoes and fry them golden brown in a pan.

25375.q: Which part of the potato plant do we eat?
25375.e: We eat the tubers that grow underground. The plant’s green berries are poisonous.
25375.m: The part of the potato we eat is the tuber.

25377.q: Why did the potato become so important in Europe?
a: It is filling and grows well
25377.e: Potatoes grow even in cool places and give a big harvest. So they helped against hunger.
25377.m: The potato helped fight hunger in Europe.

25378.q: Which continent does the tomato come from?
25378.e: The tomato originally grew in Central and South America. It only came to Europe after the voyages of discovery.

25379.q: What were tomatoes often grown for in Europe at first?
25379.e: At first many people thought the tomato was poisonous. So for a long time it was only grown for decoration.
25379.m: In Europe, the tomato was first an ornamental plant.

25380.q: Which plant is the tomato related to?
25380.e: The tomato and the potato both belong to the nightshade family.
25380.m: The tomato and the potato are related.

25381.q: What is a tomato really, according to botany?
25381.e: The tomato grows from the flower and contains seeds. That is why experts call it a fruit, more precisely a berry.
25381.m: The tomato is actually a fruit.

25382.e: People in Mexico bred maize from a wild grass thousands of years ago.

25383.q: Which dish from Ticino is made from maize semolina?
25383.e: Polenta is a porridge made from maize semolina. People in Ticino especially like eating it.

25384.q: Which snack is made by heating maize kernels?
25384.e: There is a little water inside a maize kernel. When it is heated, the kernel bursts open, and that makes popcorn.
25384.m: Popcorn is made from maize kernels.

25385.q: What is the part of the maize plant called where the kernels sit?
25385.e: The yellow kernels sit tightly packed on a cob.
25385.m: Maize kernels grow on a cob.

25386.q: Which illness often plagued sailors on long voyages?
25386.e: On long voyages many sailors got scurvy. Many died of it.
25386.m: Scurvy was a feared disease among sailors.

25387.q: What were sailors lacking when they got scurvy?
25387.e: Scurvy develops when the body gets too little vitamin C. There was no fresh fruit or vegetables on board.
25387.m: Scurvy comes from too little vitamin C.

25388.e: Lemons and limes contain a lot of vitamin C. That is why they protect against scurvy.

25389.q: What happens to the gums with scurvy?
25389.e: With scurvy the gums become soft and bleed. Later, teeth may even fall out.

25390.q: Which food did James Cook take on his ships against scurvy?
25390.e: Cook had lots of sauerkraut brought on board. It keeps for a long time and contains some vitamin C.

25391.q: Which hard bread did sailors eat on long voyages?
25391.e: Ship’s biscuits were baked very dry and hard. That is why they kept for a long time.

25392.q: What did many sailors sleep in on board?
25392.e: Hammocks took up little space. They swung with the ship and you did not fall out.

25393.q: Where was drinking water kept on board?
25393.e: The water was stored in wooden barrels. After a while it often became dirty and went bad.
25393.m: Drinking water was stored in wooden barrels.

25394.q: Which country did the seafarer Bartolomeu Dias come from?
25394.e: Bartolomeu Dias was a seafarer from Portugal. He sailed for the Portuguese king.

25395.q: What did Bartolomeu Dias manage as the first European in 1488?
a: He sailed around the southern tip of Africa
25395.e: In 1488 Dias sailed around the southern tip of Africa. This showed that you could carry on east this way.
25395.m: Dias was the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa.

25396.q: What name did Bartolomeu Dias first give the cape, because of the bad weather?
25396.e: Dias met fierce storms there, so he called it the “Cape of Storms”.
25396.m: Dias first called it the Cape of Storms.

25397.q: What is the cape near Cape Town that Bartolomeu Dias saw called today?
25397.e: The Portuguese king gave the cape a new name. He now hoped for a sea route to India.
25397.m: The Cape of Good Hope is near Cape Town.

25398.q: In which present-day country is the Cape of Good Hope?
25398.e: The Cape of Good Hope is right in the south of Africa, in the country of South Africa.
25398.m: The Cape of Good Hope is in South Africa.

25399.q: Why did Bartolomeu Dias turn back after the cape?
a: His crew wanted to go home
25399.e: The sailors were tired and afraid. So Dias had to turn back without reaching India.
25399.m: Dias turned back because his men wanted to go home.

25400.q: Which country did the seafarer Abel Tasman come from?
25400.e: Abel Tasman was Dutch. He sailed for a Dutch trading company.

25401.q: Which island south of Australia is named after Abel Tasman?
25401.e: Tasman reached the island in 1642. Later it was named Tasmania after him.
25401.m: Tasmania is named after Abel Tasman.

25402.q: Which country did Abel Tasman become the first European to see in 1642?
25402.e: In December 1642 Abel Tasman became the first European to see the coast of New Zealand.
25402.m: Tasman was the first European to see New Zealand.

25403.q: What is the sea between Australia and New Zealand called?
25403.e: The sea between Australia and New Zealand bears Abel Tasman’s name.
25403.m: The Tasman Sea lies between Australia and New Zealand.

25404.q: Who did Abel Tasman sail for?
25404.e: Tasman sailed for the Dutch East India Company. This company traded in spices.
25404.m: Abel Tasman sailed for a trading company.

25405.q: In which century did Abel Tasman live?
25405.e: Tasman made his great voyage in 1642. That belongs to the 17th century.
25405.m: Abel Tasman lived in the 17th century.

25406.q: Which national park in New Zealand bears the seafarer’s name?
25406.e: The Abel Tasman National Park is in the north of New Zealand’s South Island.
25406.m: A national park in New Zealand is named after Abel Tasman.

25407.q: Which part of the world is missing on the Behaim Globe of 1492, the oldest surviving globe of the Earth?
25407.e: The globe was finished in 1492, the same year Columbus sailed to America. Europeans did not yet know about America then, so it is missing from the globe.
25407.m: America is missing from the oldest globe, from 1492.

25408.q: What did the Behaim Globe of 1492 show about the shape of the Earth?
a: The Earth is a flat disc.
25408.e: Educated people had known for a long time that the Earth is round. A globe therefore shows the Earth as a sphere. The Behaim Globe was made in Nuremberg.
25408.m: A globe shows the Earth as a sphere.

25409.q: Which continent is missing on Martin Behaim’s globe?
25409.e: The globe was finished before people in Europe knew about America. So where America lies, there is mostly sea.
25409.m: America is missing from the Behaim Globe.

25410.q: What was Martin Behaim’s globe also called in German?
25410.e: Because of its round shape, the globe was called the “Erdapfel”, which means “earth apple”.
25410.m: The Behaim Globe is also called the Erdapfel (earth apple).

25412.q: In which country is the city of Nuremberg, where the Behaim Globe is kept today?
25412.e: Nuremberg is a city in Bavaria in Germany. The globe is in the Germanic National Museum.
25412.m: The Behaim Globe is in Germany.

25413.e: Gerardus Mercator drew maps and made globes. He was one of the most famous cartographers.

25414.q: In which year did Gerardus Mercator draw his famous world map?
25414.e: Mercator presented his large world map in 1569.

25415.q: Who found Mercator’s world map particularly useful?
25415.e: On Mercator’s map, sailors could draw their course as a straight line.

25416.q: Which land looks far too big on the Mercator map?
25416.e: The closer a land is to the poles, the bigger it looks. That is why Greenland looks huge.
25416.m: On the Mercator map, Greenland looks far too big.

25417.q: Which word for a book with many maps goes back to Mercator?
25417.e: Mercator called his collection of maps an “Atlas”. Map books are still called that today.
25417.m: An atlas is a book with many maps.

25418.q: Why can a flat map never show the Earth completely correctly?
25418.e: You cannot spread out a sphere flat without distorting it. That is why sizes or shapes on flat maps are never quite right.
25418.m: A sphere cannot be drawn flat without errors.

25419.q: In which German city did Gerardus Mercator live for many years?
25419.e: Mercator moved to Duisburg in 1552. He worked there until his death.
25419.m: Mercator lived in Duisburg for a long time.

25420.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
25420.e: Michelangelo painted the huge ceiling from 1508 to 1512. The Pope had given him the job.
25420.m: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

25421.q: In which small state is the Sistine Chapel?
25421.e: The chapel is part of the Pope’s palace. The Vatican is a tiny state in the middle of Rome.
25421.m: The Sistine Chapel is in the Vatican.

25422.q: Which ceiling painting shows God and Adam with their fingers almost touching?
25422.e: In this painting God reaches out his hand towards Adam. The fingers that almost touch are world-famous.
25422.m: The Creation of Adam is the chapel’s best-known ceiling painting.

25423.q: About how long did Michelangelo spend painting the ceiling?
25423.e: He began in 1508 and finished in 1512. Working high up was very tiring.
25423.m: Michelangelo worked on the ceiling for about four years.

25424.q: Which famous marble statue did Michelangelo create in Florence?
25424.e: Michelangelo was also a sculptor. His statue of David is over 5 metres tall.
25424.m: Michelangelo carved the statue of David.

25425.q: Whom do the cardinals elect in the Sistine Chapel?
25425.e: When a new pope is elected, the cardinals meet in this chapel. White smoke shows that the election has succeeded.
25425.m: The Pope is elected in the Sistine Chapel.

25426.q: Which huge picture did Michelangelo later paint on the altar wall of the chapel?
25426.e: The Last Judgement was painted many years after the ceiling. It covers the whole wall behind the altar.
25426.m: The Last Judgement decorates the chapel’s altar wall.

25427.q: What did Michelangelo stand on when he painted the high ceiling?
25427.e: He had tall wooden scaffolding built. That way he could get close to the ceiling.
25427.m: Michelangelo painted the ceiling from scaffolding.

25428.q: What do you paint on when making a fresco?
25428.e: For a fresco, paint is put on damp plaster. As it dries, the paint bonds firmly with the wall.
25428.m: A fresco is painted on wet plaster.

25429.q: Which planet did Galileo see with strange “ears”, which were later recognised as rings?
25429.e: Galileo’s telescope was not yet sharp enough. He saw two bulges on Saturn; only later were the rings recognised.
25429.m: Galileo was the first to see something of Saturn’s rings.

25430.q: Which planet did the space probe Galileo fly to?
25430.e: The space probe Galileo launched in 1989 and flew to Jupiter. It studied the planet and its moons, which Galileo had discovered.
25430.m: The Galileo space probe explored Jupiter.

25431.q: At which university in Italy did Galileo teach for many years?
25431.e: Galileo was a professor in Padua from 1592 to 1610. He also made his first telescope observations there.
25431.m: Galileo taught in Padua for a long time.

25432.q: What happened to Galileo’s eyes in the last years of his life?
25432.e: In old age Galileo lost his sight. Even so, he carried on working with helpers.
25432.m: Galileo went blind in old age.

25433.q: Who did Galileo come into conflict with because he said the Earth goes around the Sun?
25433.e: In 1633 Galileo had to take back his teaching before a Church court. Only much later did the Church admit he was right.
25433.m: Galileo came into conflict with the Church because of his teaching.

25434.q: In which year did Galileo begin exploring the sky with a telescope?
25434.e: In 1609 Galileo built his first telescope. Soon afterwards he made many discoveries.
25434.m: Galileo looked through his telescope from 1609 onwards.

25435.q: What is the Milky Way in the night sky made of?
25435.e: With the naked eye, the Milky Way looks like a bright band. With his telescope, Galileo saw that it consists of countless stars.
25435.m: The Milky Way is made of a huge number of stars.

25436.q: Which dark patches did Galileo observe on the Sun?
25436.e: Galileo saw dark spots moving across the Sun. Careful: never look directly at the Sun!
25436.m: There are dark sunspots on the Sun.

25437.q: What did Galileo study by watching a weight swinging back and forth?
25437.e: Galileo noticed that a pendulum always takes the same time for one swing. This later helped in building pendulum clocks.
25437.m: Galileo studied how a pendulum swings.

25438.q: According to Nicolaus Copernicus, what is at the centre of our planetary system?
25438.e: Copernicus realised that the planets go around the Sun. The Earth is one of these planets too.
25438.m: According to Copernicus, the Sun is at the centre.

25439.q: Which country did Copernicus come from?
25439.e: Copernicus was born in 1473 in Thorn, which belonged to Poland. Today the town is called Toruń.

25440.q: What did most people believe before Copernicus?
a: The Earth stands still at the centre
25440.e: People thought the Sun, Moon and stars turned around the motionless Earth. Copernicus questioned this idea.
25440.m: People used to believe the Earth was at the centre.

25441.q: Which job did Copernicus also do besides studying the stars?
25441.e: Copernicus had studied medicine and treated sick people. He also worked for the Church.

25442.q: What did Nicolaus Copernicus claim about the Earth?
a: It is the centre of the universe
It stands still and the stars do not move
25442.e: People used to believe that the Sun went around the Earth. Copernicus explained that the Earth and the other planets go around the Sun.
25442.m: Copernicus realised that the Earth goes around the Sun.

25443.q: As Copernicus explained, what causes day and night?
a: The Earth spins on its axis
25443.e: The Earth spins once a day on its own axis. The side facing the Sun has day.
25443.m: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.

25444.q: What on the Moon bears Copernicus’s name?
25444.e: Many craters on the Moon are named after famous scientists. The crater Copernicus can even be seen with binoculars.
25444.m: A crater on the Moon is named after Copernicus.

25445.q: Which force makes an apple fall from a tree to the ground?
25445.e: The Earth pulls all things towards it. Isaac Newton described this force precisely.
25445.m: Gravity pulls things towards the Earth.

25446.q: What did Newton explain with the Moon’s pull?
25446.e: The Moon pulls on the water of the seas. That is why the sea rises and falls twice a day on many coasts.

25447.q: At which famous English university did Newton study and teach?
25447.e: Newton studied at Cambridge and became a professor of mathematics there. He stayed at this university for many years.
25447.m: Newton did his research at the University of Cambridge.

25448.q: According to Newton, what keeps the Moon on its path around the Earth?
25448.e: Newton realised that the same force that makes the apple fall also holds the Moon in place. Without it, the Moon would fly away.
25448.m: Gravity keeps the Moon near the Earth.

25449.q: What did Newton split white light into using a glass prism?
25449.e: Newton let sunlight pass through a prism. Behind it, all the colours of the rainbow appeared.
25449.m: White light is made of all the colours of the rainbow.

25451.q: Which telescope did Newton build with a mirror instead of glass lenses?
25451.e: Around 1668 Newton built a telescope with a curved mirror. Large telescopes still work like this today.

25452.q: Why can an astronaut jump much higher on the Moon than on the Earth?
a: There is a strong wind there
25452.e: The Moon is much smaller than the Earth and pulls less strongly. That is why you weigh less there.
25452.m: Gravity is weaker on the Moon.

25453.q: What did Johannes Kepler describe with his famous laws?
25453.e: Kepler calculated exactly how the planets move around the Sun. His laws still apply today.
25453.m: Kepler described the orbits of the planets.

25454.q: According to Kepler, what shape are the planets’ orbits?
25454.e: Before Kepler, people thought planets moved in exact circles. Kepler showed that they are ellipses, that is, slightly stretched circles.
25454.m: Planets orbit the Sun in ellipses.

25455.q: Which country did Johannes Kepler come from?
25455.e: Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt in Württemberg. That is in present-day Germany.

25456.q: Which astronomer from Denmark did Kepler work with in Prague?
25456.e: Tycho Brahe had observed the planets very precisely. Kepler used his measurements for his laws.

25457.q: What did the space telescope named after Kepler look for?
25457.e: The Kepler space telescope launched in 2009. It found thousands of planets orbiting other stars.
25457.m: The Kepler telescope looked for planets around other stars.

25458.q: What did Kepler improve so that people could observe the sky better?
25458.e: Kepler suggested a telescope with two curved lenses. It shows a bigger image than the older telescope.

25459.q: According to Kepler, when does a planet move fastest?
a: When it is close to the Sun
When it is far from the Sun
When it is night on Earth
25459.e: Kepler found that planets move faster near the Sun. Further away they slow down.
25459.m: Planets are faster when close to the Sun.

25460.q: What did Johannes Kepler mainly study?
25460.e: Kepler was an astronomer. He calculated how the planets move around the Sun.
25460.m: Kepler studied the orbits of the planets.

25461.q: Which animal did Albrecht Dürer paint so realistically in 1502 that you can see every hair?
25461.e: The picture is called “Young Hare”. It is one of the most famous animal pictures in the world.
25461.m: Dürer painted a very realistic hare.

25462.q: Which famous drawing by Dürer shows two hands?
25462.e: “Praying Hands” is a drawing by Dürer. Today you can find it on many cards and pictures.

25463.q: Whom did Dürer paint again and again, as one of the first artists to do so?
25463.e: Dürer painted several self-portraits. That was something new at the time.
25463.m: Dürer painted many pictures of himself.

25464.q: Which technique allowed Dürer to print a picture many times?
25464.e: For a woodcut, the picture is carved into a wooden block. Afterwards it can be printed on paper again and again.
25464.m: With a woodcut, pictures can be printed many times.

25465.q: Which animal did Dürer draw in 1515, even though he had never seen one himself?
25465.e: Dürer only had a description and a sketch. That is why his rhinoceros wears a kind of armour.
25465.m: Dürer drew a rhinoceros without ever having seen one.

25466.q: Which country did Dürer travel to in order to get to know the new art of the Renaissance?
25466.e: Dürer travelled over the Alps to Venice. There he learned a lot from the Italian painters.
25466.m: Dürer got to know the Renaissance in Italy.

25467.q: In which Swiss city did the young Dürer work around 1492?
25467.e: As a young journeyman, Dürer travelled around. In Basel he made pictures for printed books.
25467.m: The young Dürer worked in Basel.

25468.q: With which two letters did Dürer sign his works?
25468.e: Dürer put a large A with a small D underneath on his pictures. That is his mark.
25468.m: Dürer signed with the letters AD.

25469.q: With which device did Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discover tiny living things?
25469.e: Leeuwenhoek built small microscopes himself. With them he saw things you cannot see with the naked eye.
25469.m: Leeuwenhoek did his research with a microscope.

25470.q: Which country did Leeuwenhoek come from?
25470.e: Leeuwenhoek lived in the town of Delft. It is in the Netherlands.

25471.q: What did Leeuwenhoek see when he looked at a drop of water under the microscope?
25471.e: Lots of tiny creatures were swimming in the drop. He called them “little animals”.
25471.m: Tiny living things live in a drop of water.

25472.q: What job did Leeuwenhoek have before he became famous?
25472.e: Leeuwenhoek sold fabrics. He checked the threads with magnifying glasses, and that is how he came to the microscope.
25472.m: Leeuwenhoek was originally a cloth merchant.

a: It makes small things look big
It makes distant things look close
25473.e: A microscope magnifies very small things. That way you can look at them closely.

25474.q: What did Leeuwenhoek find in the plaque on his teeth?
25474.e: He scraped plaque off his teeth and saw tiny living things. Today we know they were bacteria.

25475.q: How many lenses did most of Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes have?
25475.e: His microscopes usually had only one tiny, very finely ground lens. Even so, some magnified more than 200 times.
25475.m: Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes had only one lens.

25476.q: What did Leeuwenhoek observe in blood?
25476.e: Leeuwenhoek described red blood cells very precisely. They give blood its red colour.
25476.m: Red blood cells float in the blood.

25477.q: Into which language did Martin Luther translate the Bible?
25477.e: Before that, the Bible in church was mostly in Latin. Luther wanted everyone to be able to read it.
25477.m: Luther translated the Bible into German.

25478.q: Which invention helped spread Luther’s writings quickly everywhere?
25478.e: With printing, Luther’s Bible and writings could be produced quickly in large numbers. Johannes Gutenberg had invented it around 1450.

25479.q: From which language did Luther translate the New Testament?
25479.e: The New Testament was originally written in Greek. Luther translated from this text.
25479.m: Luther translated the New Testament from Greek.

25480.q: Roughly how long did Luther take to translate the New Testament?
25480.e: Luther worked very fast and was finished after about eleven weeks. For the whole Bible, he and his helpers needed many years.
25480.m: Luther translated the New Testament in about eleven weeks.

25481.q: How did Luther want to translate so that everyone would understand him?
25481.e: Luther said you had to listen to how ordinary people really talk. He chose words that everyone knew.
25481.m: Luther translated into the language of the people.

25482.q: Under which false name did Luther live in hiding at the castle?
25482.e: Luther let his hair and beard grow. As “Junker Jörg”, nobody recognised him.

25483.q: According to legend, what did Luther throw at the Devil in the castle?
25483.e: That is what an old legend says. The story is probably made up, but it is very well known.
25483.m: According to legend, Luther threw an inkpot at the Devil.

25484.q: Which reformer in Zurich also published a Bible in German?
25484.e: In 1531 the whole Bible was published in German in Zurich. Zwingli and his helpers had translated it.
25484.m: Zwingli published a German Bible in Zurich.

25485.q: Who is considered the inventor of the pocket watch?
25485.e: Around 1510 the locksmith Peter Henlein built small clocks that people could carry around. That is why he is considered the inventor of the pocket watch.
25485.m: Peter Henlein is considered the inventor of the pocket watch.

25486.q: Where did men use to carry their pocket watch?
25486.e: The pocket watch was usually kept in a small pocket of the waistcoat. You took it out to read the time.
25486.m: The pocket watch was kept in the waistcoat pocket.

25487.q: What was a pocket watch attached to so that it would not get lost?
25487.e: The watch was kept in the waistcoat pocket. A chain connected it to the clothes.
25487.m: A pocket watch often hangs on a chain.

25488.q: What powers a mechanical pocket watch?
25488.e: Inside the watch there is a spring that you wind up. As it unwinds, it moves the hands.
25488.m: A spring powers a mechanical watch.

25489.q: What did you regularly have to do with an old pocket watch to keep it going?
25489.e: To wind it, you turn a little wheel called the crown. Otherwise the watch stops after a while.
25489.m: An old pocket watch has to be wound up.

25490.q: Which two towns in the canton of Neuchâtel are World Heritage Sites because of watchmaking?
25490.e: Both towns were built entirely around the needs of watchmakers. They have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 2009.
25490.m: La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are watchmaking towns.

25491.q: In which region of Switzerland have there long been especially many watchmakers?
25491.e: Many watch workshops grew up in the Jura arc from Geneva to Basel. Swiss watches are famous all over the world.
25491.m: There are many watchmakers in the Jura.

25492.q: Which kind of watch later replaced the pocket watch?
25492.e: In the 20th century more and more people wore their watch on their wrist. That was more practical than in a pocket.
25492.m: The wristwatch replaced the pocket watch.

25493.q: Which country did William Shakespeare come from?
25493.e: Shakespeare was an English writer. He lived and worked mainly in London.

25494.q: In which small town was Shakespeare born?
25494.e: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564. You can visit the house where he was born today.

25495.q: Which play by Shakespeare tells the story of a young couple in love from Verona?
25495.e: Romeo and Juliet love each other, but their families are enemies. The story is very sad.
25495.m: Romeo and Juliet is a play by Shakespeare.

25496.q: What was the name of the famous round theatre in London where Shakespeare’s plays were performed?
25496.e: The Globe Theatre was a round wooden theatre. A reconstruction stands in London again today.
25496.m: Shakespeare’s plays were performed at the Globe Theatre.

25497.e: Shakespeare wrote comedies, tragedies and poems. His plays are performed all over the world.

25498.q: Which play does the line “To be, or not to be” come from?
25498.e: Prince Hamlet says this line while he is thinking. It is one of the best-known lines in the world.
25498.m: The line “To be, or not to be” comes from Hamlet.

25499.q: In which play by Shakespeare do fairies get up to mischief in a magic forest?
25499.e: “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” features fairies and a sprite called Puck. It is a funny comedy.
25499.m: Fairies appear in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.

25500.q: In Shakespeare’s time, who played the female roles in the theatre?
25500.e: Women were not allowed to act on stage in England at that time. So boys took the female roles.
25500.m: In Shakespeare’s time, boys played the female roles.

25501.q: Which country did the painter Raphael come from?
25501.e: Raphael was born in Urbino in Italy in 1483. Later he painted in Florence and Rome.
25501.m: Raphael was a painter from Italy.

25502.q: Which famous wall painting by Raphael shows many scholars of ancient Greece?
25502.e: In the painting, thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle stand in a great hall. It is one of the most famous wall paintings in the world.
25502.m: Raphael painted The School of Athens.

25503.q: What can you see right at the bottom of Raphael’s painting “Sistine Madonna”?
25503.e: The two thoughtful little angels are world-famous. You can find them on many postcards.
25503.m: Two angels sit at the bottom of the Sistine Madonna.

25504.q: What did Raphael paint especially often?
25504.e: Raphael painted many Madonnas, that is, pictures of Mary with the baby Jesus. They look gentle and kind.
25504.m: Raphael painted many pictures of Mary with the child.

25505.q: How old was Raphael when he died?
25505.e: Raphael lived from 1483 to 1520. So he died at only 37.

25506.q: For whom did Raphael decorate magnificent rooms in the Vatican?
25506.e: The Pope brought Raphael to Rome. Today the rooms are called the “Raphael Rooms”.
25506.m: Raphael decorated rooms for the Pope.

25507.q: Which two artists, together with Raphael, are counted among the greatest painters of the High Renaissance?
25507.e: Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael lived at the same time. All three worked in Italy.
25507.m: Raphael, Leonardo and Michelangelo are great masters.

25508.e: His father, Giovanni Santi, was a painter and poet. Raphael learned from him from an early age.
25508.m: Raphael’s father was a painter too.

25509.e: The word comes from French. It refers to a rebirth of ancient knowledge.

25510.q: Which ancient art did people admire again during the Renaissance?
a: The art of the ancient Greeks and Romans
The art of the ancient Egyptians
25510.e: People admired the works of antiquity again. Artists and scholars learned from the ancient Greeks and Romans.
25510.m: In the Renaissance, the art of antiquity came back to life.

25511.q: Which invention around 1450 helped spread new knowledge quickly?
25511.e: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type. Now books could be produced much faster.

25512.q: Which rich banking family supported many artists during the Renaissance?
25512.e: The Medici were very rich bankers. They gave artists commissions and money.

25513.q: Who painted the famous picture “Mona Lisa”?
25513.e: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter, inventor and scientist. The Mona Lisa now hangs in the Louvre in Paris.
25513.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.

25514.e: The Renaissance lasted roughly from the 15th into the 16th century. That is about 200 years.
25514.m: The Renaissance was roughly from 1400 to 1600.

25515.q: What did Renaissance painters learn so that their pictures would look three-dimensional and deep?
25515.e: With perspective, things further back are painted smaller. This makes a flat picture look deep.

25516.q: Which period came directly before the Renaissance?
25516.e: Before the Renaissance came the Middle Ages. The early modern period begins with the Renaissance.
25516.m: The Middle Ages came before the Renaissance.

25517.q: Which famous Renaissance painter worked in Basel for a long time?
25517.e: In Basel, Holbein painted portraits and altarpieces. Many of his works hang in the Kunstmuseum Basel today.
25517.m: Hans Holbein the Younger worked in Basel.

25518.q: Which country did Louis XIV rule?
25518.e: Louis XIV was King of France. He belonged to the Bourbon family.
25518.m: Louis XIV was King of France.

25519.q: Under Louis XIV, who decided almost everything in France alone?
25519.e: Louis XIV ruled as an absolute monarch. He made the important decisions alone, and nobody was allowed to contradict him.
25519.m: Louis XIV ruled France almost entirely on his own.

25520.q: In which country is the Palace of Versailles?
25520.e: The Palace of Versailles is in France. It is one of the most famous palaces in the world.
25520.m: The Palace of Versailles is in France.

25521.q: What lies all around the Palace of Versailles?
25521.e: Behind the palace is a huge garden with paths, ponds and many fountains. It was laid out very neatly and in straight lines.
25521.m: Versailles is surrounded by a large park with many fountains.

25522.q: Apart from the royal family, who lived in the Palace of Versailles?
25522.e: Louis XIV brought many nobles to his court at Versailles. On top of that there were thousands of servants, cooks and craftsmen.
25522.m: Many nobles and servants lived at the court of Versailles.

25523.q: What did fine gentlemen at the court of Louis XIV wear on their heads?
25523.e: At court, fine gentlemen wore long, curly wigs. That was the great fashion of the time.
25523.m: Fine gentlemen wore large curly wigs back then.

25524.q: What was often used to make wigs white?
25524.e: Wigs were dusted with powder, often made from starch or flour. This made them white or grey.

25525.q: What did a large, expensive wig show other people?
a: That someone was rich and important
25525.e: Large wigs were expensive and took a lot of work. Anyone wearing one showed that they were rich and important.

a: A wide skirt with hoops underneath
25526.e: Round hoops are sewn in underneath a hoop skirt. This makes the skirt stand out wide from the body.
25526.m: A hoop skirt is a wide skirt with hoops.

25527.q: What did fine ladies wear tightly around their upper body under their dress?
25527.e: A corset was laced up tightly. This made the waist look especially slim.
25527.m: A corset made the waist look slim.

25528.q: What colour were the heels on Louis XIV’s shoes?
25528.e: Louis XIV wore shoes with red heels. Only he and nobles he allowed could wear such shoes.
25528.m: Louis XIV wore shoes with red heels.

25529.q: In which present-day country is Mozart’s home town?
25529.e: Salzburg is in Austria today. That is why Mozart is regarded as a famous Austrian composer.
25529.m: Mozart’s home town is in Austria.

25530.q: About how old was Mozart when he wrote his first pieces of music?
25530.e: Mozart was already writing little pieces at about 5 years old. That is why he is called a child prodigy.
25530.m: Mozart was a musical child prodigy.

25531.q: What was Mozart’s older sister, who made music with him, called?
25531.e: His sister Maria Anna was called Nannerl. The two children played together for kings and princes.
25531.m: Mozart’s sister Nannerl made music with him.

25532.q: Who was Mozart’s father and first music teacher?
25532.e: Leopold Mozart was a musician himself. He taught his children and travelled around Europe with them.
25532.m: Leopold Mozart was Wolfgang’s father and teacher.

25533.q: Which Swiss city did the young Mozart visit on a journey in 1766?
25533.e: On their way home in 1766 the Mozart family also travelled through Switzerland. They gave concerts in Zurich, for example.
25533.m: The young Mozart gave concerts in Zurich in 1766.

25534.q: Which well-known piece of music is by Mozart?
25534.e: Mozart wrote “Eine kleine Nachtmusik” (A Little Night Music) in 1787. Many people know its cheerful tune.

25535.q: Which present-day country did Johann Sebastian Bach come from?
25535.e: Bach was born in Eisenach, a town in present-day Germany. He lived and worked in German lands all his life.
25535.m: Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer.

25536.q: For which large church instrument is Bach especially famous?
25536.e: Bach was a brilliant organist. He wrote many pieces for the church organ.

25537.q: Roughly how many children did Johann Sebastian Bach have?
25537.e: Bach had 20 children with his two wives. But many of them died as babies.

25538.q: In which city did Bach work for a long time as cantor of St Thomas Church?
25538.e: From 1723 Bach was cantor of St Thomas in Leipzig. There he led the boys’ choir and wrote music for church services.
25538.m: Bach was cantor of St Thomas in Leipzig.

25539.q: Which famous work for the Christmas season did Bach write?
25539.e: The Christmas Oratorio tells the story of Jesus’s birth through music. Bach wrote it in 1734. “Messiah” was written by Handel.

25540.q: In which year was Johann Sebastian Bach born?
25540.e: Bach was born on 21 March 1685. So he lived over 300 years ago.
25540.m: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in 1685.

25541.q: What job did many of Johann Sebastian Bach’s relatives have?
25541.e: The Bach family was a real family of musicians. Several of his sons also became well-known composers.
25541.m: There were many musicians in the Bach family.

25542.q: What happened to Beethoven’s hearing as he got older?
25542.e: Beethoven’s hearing got worse and worse until he was completely deaf. Even so, he carried on composing.
25542.m: Beethoven went deaf and still kept on composing.

25543.q: In which city did Beethoven live for most of his life?
25543.e: In 1792 Beethoven moved to Vienna. He stayed there until his death in 1827.
25543.m: Beethoven lived in Vienna for a long time.

25544.q: Which famous piano piece by Beethoven has a girl’s name in its title?
25544.e: “Für Elise” (For Elise) is one of the best-known piano pieces in the world. Many children learn it in piano lessons.
25544.m: “Für Elise” is a piano piece by Beethoven.

25545.q: On which instrument was Beethoven a great master?
25545.e: Beethoven was a brilliant pianist. In Vienna he thrilled people with his piano playing.

25546.q: How many symphonies did Beethoven write?
25546.e: Beethoven wrote 9 symphonies. The last one, the 9th Symphony, is especially famous.

25547.q: How could Beethoven compose even though he could no longer hear anything?
a: He heard the music in his head
25547.e: Beethoven knew the notes so well that he could imagine them in his head. So he wrote the music down without hearing it.
25547.m: Beethoven heard the music in his head.

25548.q: Which empire did Maria Theresa rule?
25548.e: From 1740 Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg lands, with Austria at their heart. She was one of the most powerful women of her time.

25549.q: How many children did Maria Theresa have?
25549.e: Maria Theresa had 16 children. Many of her daughters married kings and princes all over Europe.

25550.q: Which daughter of Maria Theresa became Queen of France?
25550.e: Marie Antoinette married the heir to the French throne in 1770. From 1774 she was Queen of France.
25550.m: Marie Antoinette was a daughter of Maria Theresa.

25551.q: Which palace in Vienna did Maria Theresa have extended as her summer residence?
25551.e: Maria Theresa had Schönbrunn Palace splendidly rebuilt. It is in Vienna and is a World Heritage Site today.
25551.m: Schönbrunn Palace was Maria Theresa’s favourite palace.

25552.q: What did Maria Theresa introduce for all children in 1774?
25552.e: In 1774 Maria Theresa introduced compulsory schooling for all. Children now had to go to school for at least six years.

25553.q: Which famous ruling family did Maria Theresa belong to?
25553.e: Maria Theresa was a Habsburg. The Habsburg family originally came from Aargau in Switzerland.
25553.m: Maria Theresa belonged to the Habsburg family.

25554.q: Which silver coin with Maria Theresa’s portrait was still being minted long after her death?
25554.e: The Maria Theresa thaler shows her portrait. It was so popular that it was still being minted long after her death.
25554.m: The Maria Theresa thaler shows Maria Theresa.

25555.q: What did the Montgolfier brothers invent?
25555.e: The brothers Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier built the first hot-air balloon in 1783.
25555.m: The Montgolfier brothers invented the hot-air balloon.

25556.q: Which country did the Montgolfier brothers come from?
25556.e: The Montgolfier brothers came from Annonay in France. That is where they launched their first balloon.

25557.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
a: Warm air is lighter than cold air
25557.e: Warm air is lighter than the cold air outside. That is why the balloon full of hot air rises.

25558.q: Which animals were the first passengers in a hot-air balloon in 1783?
a: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel
A dog, a cat and a mouse
A horse, a cow and a goat
A monkey, a hare and a goose
25558.e: At Versailles a sheep, a duck and a cockerel flew in the basket. All three survived the short flight.
25558.m: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel were the first to fly in a balloon.

25559.q: In which year did the Montgolfier brothers’ first hot-air balloons go up?
25559.e: In 1783 the brothers launched their balloons in public. In the same year the first people flew too.
25559.m: The hot-air balloon first flew in 1783.

25560.q: How did the Montgolfier family earn their money?
25560.e: The family owned a paper factory. That is why the brothers built their balloons from cloth and paper.

25561.q: Over which city did people fly in a hot-air balloon for the first time in November 1783?
25561.e: On 21 November 1783 two men flew over Paris. They were in the air for about 25 minutes.
25561.m: The first people flew over Paris in 1783.

25562.q: Which prison in Paris did the people storm at the beginning of the Revolution?
25562.e: In summer 1789 Parisians stormed the Bastille. It was a symbol of the King’s power.

25563.q: On which day does France celebrate its national holiday today?
25563.e: The holiday commemorates the start of the Revolution in 1789. On this day there are parades and fireworks in France.

25565.q: What colours is the flag that has stood for France since the Revolution?
25565.e: The French flag has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red. It is called the Tricolore.
25565.m: The French flag is blue, white and red.

25566.q: What is the French national anthem that was written during the Revolution called?
25566.e: La Marseillaise was written in 1792. Soldiers from Marseille sang it in Paris, which is where the name comes from.
25566.m: La Marseillaise is the anthem of France.

25568.q: Which country did Peter the Great rule?
25568.e: Peter the Great ruled Russia from 1682. He wanted to make his country more modern.

25569.q: What title did Russian rulers such as Peter the Great have?
25569.e: The rulers of Russia were called tsars. Peter later also took the title of emperor.
25569.m: Peter the Great was a Russian tsar.

25570.q: Which craft did Peter the Great learn on a journey to Holland?
25570.e: In disguise, Peter worked in a shipyard in Holland. He wanted to learn how to build good ships.
25570.m: Peter the Great learned shipbuilding in Holland.

25571.q: Under Peter the Great, what did Russian men have to pay if they wanted to keep a beard?
25571.e: Peter wanted Russians to look like Western Europeans. Anyone who wanted to keep his beard had to pay a beard tax.
25571.m: There was a beard tax under Peter the Great.

25572.q: Roughly how tall was Peter the Great?
25572.e: Peter was about 2 metres tall. So he really was a great big man.
25572.m: Peter the Great was about two metres tall.

25573.q: Which city on the Baltic Sea did Peter the Great found?
25573.e: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg on the Baltic Sea in 1703. The city became Russia’s new capital.
25573.m: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg.

25574.q: Which city did Peter the Great found?
25574.e: Peter the Great had the city built at the mouth of a river. It bears the name of his patron saint, Peter.
25574.m: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg.

25575.q: In which year was St Petersburg founded?
25575.e: St Petersburg was founded on 27 May 1703. First a fortress was built on an island.

25576.q: On which sea is St Petersburg?
25576.e: St Petersburg is on the Baltic Sea. Peter wanted a port so that Russia could trade with Western Europe.
25576.m: St Petersburg is on the Baltic Sea.

25577.q: In which country is the city of St Petersburg?
25577.e: St Petersburg is Russia’s second-largest city after Moscow. It lies in the north, by the sea.

25578.q: What role did St Petersburg have for about 200 years?
25578.e: Peter made St Petersburg the capital in 1712. Only in 1918 did Moscow become the capital again.
25578.m: St Petersburg was the capital of Russia for a long time.

25579.q: Because of its many canals, what is St Petersburg often called?
25579.e: Many canals with hundreds of bridges run through St Petersburg. That is why the city is compared with Venice.
25579.m: St Petersburg is also called the Venice of the North.

25580.q: Which country did Benjamin Franklin come from?
25580.e: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706. He was one of the founders of the United States of America.

25581.q: What did Benjamin Franklin fly in a thunderstorm to study lightning?
25581.e: According to tradition, Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm in 1752. That was very dangerous; never try anything like it!
25581.m: Franklin studied lightning with a kite.

25582.e: Benjamin Franklin’s face is on the American 100-dollar note. But he was never president.

25583.q: Which special kind of glasses is Benjamin Franklin said to have invented?
25583.e: Franklin split the lenses of his glasses into two halves. With the top part he could see into the distance, with the bottom part close up.
25583.m: Franklin had glasses for near and far.

25584.q: Which invention by Benjamin Franklin protects houses during thunderstorms?
25584.e: Franklin invented the lightning conductor around 1752. It stops lightning from setting houses on fire.
25584.m: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning conductor.

25585.q: Where does a lightning conductor send the lightning?
25585.e: The lightning conductor catches the lightning and carries it safely into the ground through a wire. That way the house is not damaged.
25585.m: The lightning conductor sends lightning into the ground.

25586.q: What material is a lightning conductor made of?
25586.e: A lightning conductor is made of metal such as copper or iron. Metal conducts electricity very well.
25586.m: A lightning conductor is made of metal.

25587.q: Where is a lightning conductor fitted?
a: In the garden under a tree
25587.e: The lightning conductor sits at the highest point of the house. That is where lightning is most likely to strike.
25587.m: The lightning conductor sits on top of the roof.

25588.q: What is lightning, as Benjamin Franklin found out?
25588.e: Franklin showed that lightning is a huge electrical discharge. That was an important discovery.

25590.q: On which day does the USA celebrate its Independence Day?
25590.e: 4 July is Independence Day in the USA. On this day there are fireworks and parades everywhere.
25590.m: The USA celebrates its birthday on 4 July.

25591.q: From which country did the American colonies want to become independent in 1776?
25591.e: The colonies belonged to Great Britain. They no longer wanted to be ruled by the British king.
25591.m: The USA broke away from Great Britain.

25592.q: Who became the first President of the USA?
25592.e: George Washington was first the leader of the army. In 1789 he became the first President of the USA.
25592.m: George Washington was the first President of the USA.

25593.q: How many colonies declared themselves independent in 1776?
25593.e: There were 13 colonies on the east coast. The 13 stripes on the US flag are a reminder of them.

25594.q: What did angry settlers throw into the sea at the “Boston Tea Party” in 1773?
25594.e: The settlers were against a tax on tea. So they threw whole chests of tea into the water in Boston harbour.
25594.m: At the Boston Tea Party, tea ended up in the sea.

25595.q: In which city was the Declaration of Independence signed?
25595.e: The representatives of the colonies met in Philadelphia. The famous Liberty Bell is there too.
25595.m: The Declaration of Independence was signed in Philadelphia.

25596.q: Which symbol did Louis XIV choose for himself?
25596.e: Louis XIV wanted to be at the centre like the Sun, with everything revolving around him. That is why you often see golden suns on his buildings.
25596.m: Louis XIV chose the Sun as his symbol.

25597.q: What is the period of Louis XIV called in art and architecture?
25597.e: In the time of Louis XIV, people built and painted in the Baroque style. Lots of gold, decoration and splendour are typical.
25597.m: Louis XIV lived in the Baroque period.

25598.q: Roughly how many rooms does the Palace of Versailles have?
25598.e: The Palace of Versailles has around 2,300 rooms. It is so big that you can get lost in it.
25598.m: The Palace of Versailles has over 2,000 rooms.

25599.q: What is there in the park at Versailles that you can go boating on?
25599.e: In the park is the Grand Canal, which is over a kilometre long. In the past, small ships even sailed there for the King.
25599.m: There is a long canal in the park at Versailles.

25600.q: What kind of hat did Napoleon usually wear?
25600.e: Napoleon wore a bicorne, a hat with two points. He often wore it sideways on his head.

25601.q: Which large gateway in Paris did Napoleon have built for his victories?
25601.e: Napoleon ordered the building of the Arc de Triomphe in 1806. It was meant to commemorate his army’s victories.
25601.m: The Arc de Triomphe in Paris commemorates Napoleon’s victories.

25602.q: What nickname did the soldiers give Napoleon?
25602.e: The soldiers fondly called Napoleon “the Little Corporal”. A corporal is a low rank in the army.
25602.m: The soldiers called Napoleon the Little Corporal.

25603.q: What were wigs often made from in the 18th century?
25603.e: Wigs were made by a special craftsman, the wigmaker. He used real human hair or animal hair, for example from horses or goats.
25603.m: Wigs were made from human or animal hair.
